Indeed, this is a astonishing thing.﴾

The meaning is: match the Qur'an with your action, and compare yourself to its obedience. Al-Hasan interpreted it this way, i.e., "Look where your deeds stand in relation to it?"

The majority said it is the well-known letter of the alphabet (ḥarf al-muʿjam), and what applies to the openings of other surahs of opinions applies to it. This position has the specific view that some people said its meaning is: "Muhammad (ﷺ) has spoken truly." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said its meaning is: "Allah has spoken truly." Mujahid ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said it is the key to the names of Allah: "Ṣamad (the Eternal), Ṣādiq al-waʿd (the Truthful in promise), Ṣāniʿ al-maṣnūʿāt (the Maker of created things)."

The majority read it with a sukun on the dal. Ibn Abi Ishaq, according to one report from him, read it with a kasra and tanwin [Ṣādin], as an oath, as you say, "By Allah, I will do it." Al-Ṭabarī and others reported from Ibn Abi Ishaq without tanwin, and he linked it to the Arab expressions ḥāth bāth and khāz bāz. A group, among them ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, read [Ṣādā] with a fatḥa on the dal, and he did this in pronouncing all letters: he says "qāfa" and "nūna," and makes them like "ayna" and "layta." Al-Thaʿlabī said: "It was also said its meaning is: Muhammad (ﷺ) hunted the hearts, by winning them over to faith."

His exalted saying: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ is an oath. Al-Suddi, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said its meaning is: possessing lasting, eternal honour. Qatada and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: full of admonition for people and guidance for them. A group said its meaning is: full of mention of the nations, the stories, and the unseen matters. As for the answer to the oath, it has been disputed. One group said the answer is in His saying "Sad," since it means: "Muhammad has spoken truly," or "Allah has spoken truly." The Kufans and al-Zajjaj said the answer is His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ [Sad: 64]. Some of the Basrans, including al-Akhfash, said the answer is in His saying: ﴿There is none but that he denied the messengers.﴾ [Sad: 14].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two opinions are far-fetched.

Qatada and al-Ṭabarī said: the answer is implied before "bal" (nay, but), and this is the correct view. Its estimate is: "By the Qur'an, the matter is not as they claim," and similar to this estimate, so consider it carefully. Al-Zajjaj related from some people that the answer is His exalted saying: ﴿How many a generation did We destroy before them﴾, and this is extremely forced.

"ʿIzza" here means contention and overpowering. "Shiqaq" is similar to it, meaning: they are in one side, and the truth is on another side.

"Kam" is for multiplication; it is a statement containing an example and a warning, and it is in the place of a direct object governed by "ahlakna" (We destroyed). "Qarn" means a community of people gathered by one time period, and its explanation has been previously discussed many times. His exalted saying: ﴿"fa-nādaw"﴾ means: calling out for help. The meaning is that they did this after witnessing (the punishment), and it did not benefit them, and it was not a time of benefit. "Wa-lāta" means "laysa" (not), and its subject is omitted according to Sibawayh, its estimate being: "wa-lāta al-ḥīnu ḥīna manāṣ" (and it was not a time of escape). It is "lā" to which a "tā'" was attached, just as it was attached to "rubbata" and "thummata." Al-Zajjaj said: it is like the tā' of "jalasat" and "qāmat," the tā' of particles like the tā' of verbs, entering upon what is indeclinable in both cases. "Lā" is not used with the tā' except with "ḥīn," "zamān," "waqt," and similar words. Among that is the poet's saying:

"Wa-lāta sāʿata mandam" (And no time for regret)

Another said:

"Tadhakkara ḥubba Layla lāta ḥīnan / wa-aḍḥā al-shayba qad qaṭaʿa al-qarīnā" (He remembered his love for Layla, but it was no longer the time, and grey hair had cut off the companion.)

(p-322) Some of them recited:

"Ṭalabū ṣulḥanā wa-lāta awānin / fa-ajabnā an laysa ḥīna baqāʾ" (They sought reconciliation with us, but it was not the time; so we answered that it was not the time for survival.)

Al-Zajjaj recited it with a kasra on the tā', and this is common. The reading of the majority is a fatḥa on the tā' of "lāta" and on the nūn of "ḥīna." It is reported from ʿĪsā a kasra on the tā' of "lātin" and a naṣb on the nūn of "ḥīna"; it is also reported from him a kasra on the nūn.

A group, and Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, paused on "lā" and joined the tā' to "ḥīn," saying "lā taḥīn." Abu ʿUbayd mentioned that it is written so in the Mushaf of ʿUthman, and he cited in support Abu Wajza's saying:

"Al-ʿāṭifūna taḥīna mā min ʿāṭifin / wa-al-muṭʿimūna zamāna mā min muṭʿimi" (They are the bestowers of kindness at a time when there is no bestower, and the feeders in a time when there is no feeder)

(p-323) He praises the family of al-Zubayr. Some people read "lāta ḥīnu" with a ḍamma on the nūn of "ḥīn," assuming an omitted predicate.

"Manāṣ" means refuge, from nāṣa yanūṣu, when one escapes and flees. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning is: it was not a time of leaping or fleeing; the people transmitted this.

The pronoun in ﴿"wa-ʿajibū"﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they found it strange that a man from among them was given prophethood, warned them, and cautioned them, and that he affirmed the oneness of God. They said: how can there be one God who provides for all and oversees all their affairs?

(p-324) "ʿUjāb" is an intensive form, as they said "sarīʿ" and "sirāʿ," and this is common. Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "ʿujjāb" with a shadda on the jim, similar to the saying of the rajiz:

"Jāʾū bi-ṣaydin ʿajabin mina al-ʿajab / uzayriqi al-ʿaynayni ṭiwāli al-dhanab" (They came with a wondrous game, of wonders, blue-eyed, long-tailed.)

And they have said: "rajulun kirām," meaning "karīm" (a generous man).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verses 6–9:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And the chiefs among them went off, saying: "Walk on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods. This is truly a thing that is intended.﴾ ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but a fabrication.﴾ ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?" Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾

It has been related in the narrative of this verse: "The nobles of Quraysh and their assembly gathered at the illness of Abu Talib, the paternal uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). They said: 'It is shameful for us that Abu Talib should die and we should then harm Muhammad, so the Arabs will say: They left him while his uncle was alive, and when he died they harmed him. Rather, let us go to Abu Talib so that he may give us justice against him, and let him bind between us and him with a firm bond.' So they rose and came to him and said: 'O Abu Talib, Muhammad reviles and mocks our opinions and the opinions of our fathers, and we will not tolerate him in that. Rather, decide between us and him during your lifetime, by having him remain in his house, worshipping the Lord whom he claims, and leaving our gods and reviling them, and not confronting anyone of us with anything of this.' So Abu Talib sent for Muhammad (ﷺ), and said: 'O Muhammad, your people have invited you to fairness, which is that you leave them and worship your Lord alone.' He said: 'Or is there something other than that, O uncle?' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'They will give you a word by which the Arabs will submit to you, and by which the non-Arabs (ʿAjam) will pay you the jizya (poll tax).' They said: 'And what is it? For we will hasten to it.' He said: 'There is no god but Allah.' Thereupon they recoiled and said: 'What else will satisfy you from us other than this?' He said: 'By Allah, if you were to give me the earth full of gold and wealth...'" And in another narration: "If you were to place the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, I would not accept anything from you other than it." Then they rose at that, and some of them were saying: "Has he made the gods one god? Indeed, this is a strange thing." They kept repeating this sentiment. And ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt was saying: ﴿Walk on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods﴾, the verse.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I have quoted this report in its complete sense. In some of its versions there is addition and omission, but the purpose is close.

"And when they had gone, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I will testify for you before Allah.' He said: 'By Allah, were it not that it would be a reproach upon my sons after me, I would have affirmed it to comfort your eye.' And he died while saying: 'Upon the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib.' So the following was revealed concerning that: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]."

As for His words in this verse, ﴿And the chiefs among them went off﴾, it is an expression for their departing from Abu Talib and their leaving that assembly. This is the view of a group of the exegetes (mufassirun). Another group said: it is an expression for their spreading these statements, as people say: "The people set out praying for the commander," and the like, meaning that their speech became widespread with it. And "al-Mala'" (the chiefs): the nobles and leaders who stand in place of the whole in opinions and the like.

As for His words ﴿أنِ امْشُوا (an imshu)﴾, "an" is explanatory (mufassira) and has no grammatical position (mawdi'). It is also possible that it has a position in the accusative (naṣb), by dropping the preposition, i.e., bi-an, so it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is as if he said: "And the chiefs among them went off with their saying: Walk on." The meaning of the verse is that some of them said to others: "Walk on and be steadfast in devotion to all the affairs of your gods." Some people held that their saying "امْشُوا (imshu)" is a supplication for the acquisition of livestock (mashiya). This is weak, because it would require that the alif be cut (in its written form as an elided hamza, i.e., the alif be maqta'a), since it is said: "amsha al-rajul" when he becomes the owner of livestock. Furthermore, this meaning does not fit the verse. Rather, the meaning is: proceed on your way and persist in your course, or the meaning is a command to move the feet, which they said upon their departure. It is in the Mushaf (codex) of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud: "And the chiefs among them went off walking, saying: be steadfast." And their saying ﴿إنَّ هَذا لَشَيْءٌ يُرادُ (inna hadha la-shay'un yuradu)﴾ means: they intend the prominence of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his exaltation through prophethood; that is, from us is demanded submission to him.

And their saying ﴿ما سَمِعْنا بِهَذا (ma sami'na bihadha)﴾ means: by the like of this statement, that God is one. The interpreters differed concerning their words ﴿فِي المِلَّةِ الآخِرَةِ (fi al-millati al-akhirati)﴾. Mujahid said: they meant their own religion and creed upon which the Arabs were, and every community's way is called a millah (religion/creed). Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi said: they meant the religion of the Christians.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

That is suitable, because it is a religion famous for the doctrine of the Trinity and that God is not one. Another group said: the meaning of their saying ﴿ما سَمِعْنا (we have not heard)﴾ is: we have not heard that the like of this would occur, nor that it is said in the last religion which we used to hear would be in the last of time.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

That is because before his mission (peace and blessings be upon him), people were sensing the emergence of a prophet and the appearance of a community and religion. What confirms the correctness of this is what has been related from the sayings of the rabbis of the monasteries (ahbar uli al-sawami'), what has been related about Shiq and Satih, and what the Children of Israel used to believe, that it would arise from among them. And their saying ﴿إنْ هَذا إلا اخْتِلاقٌ (in hadha illa ikhtilaq)﴾ is an indication of all that Muhammad (ﷺ) reports from Allah, may He be exalted.

Then they said, in the form of an affirmation from some of them to others, and this includes denial: ﴿عَلَيْهِ الذِكْرُ مِن بَيْنِنا بَلْ (ʿalayhi al-dhikru min baynina bal)﴾, meaning: we are the nobles, the notables; so why was this one singled out? And how can this be valid? So God, may He be exalted, rejected their statement with what "bal" requires, because the meaning is not that God's singling out and bestowal should follow their desires. ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِن ذِكْرِي (bal hum fi shakkin min dhikri)﴾, that is: they are in doubt about whether this reminder of God is true. Then He threatened them with His saying: ﴿بَلْ لَمّا يَذُوقُوا عَذابِ (bal lamma yadhuquʿadhabi)﴾, meaning: if they had tasted it, they would have become certain that this message is true. That is, because of their ignorance, reflection does not make it clear to them, but direct contact with the punishment makes it clear. Ibn Masʿud read: "أمْ أُنْزِلَ (am unzila)" with a mim between the two hamzas.

Then He put them to a question as a form of argument against them: Is the mercy of Allah with them, and its treasuries, in which are guidance and prophethood and every grace, so that they would have authority over the message and other blessings of Allah? And "am" here is not balanced by an alif, so it is the cut-off "am" whose meaning is a turning away from the first speech and an interrogation. Sibawayh estimated it as "bal" and the alif, like the Arabs' saying: "Innaha la-ibilun am shaʾ" (Indeed, they are camels or sheep). The "treasuries" for mercy is a metaphor, as if the meaning is: the place of its gathering and preservation, since human treasures need that; so mercy is addressed with what inclines toward that. al-Tabari said: by "al-khaza'in" he means the keys. And Allah knows best.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

"Am" (or) in this verse is equivalent to the hamzah (interrogative alif) that is implied in the first "am" (or). It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying in this verse: Or do they have this dominion, so that prophethood and messengership would be by their choosing and their judgment? ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾ if the matter is so, that is, to the heaven. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. "Al-asbab" (the means) is everything by which one reaches things, and here it means ropes and ladders. Qatadah said: He meant the gates of the heaven.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿A host there, routed﴾, the interpreters differed regarding what "there" (hunalika) refers to. One group said: it refers to climbing by the means, that is, these people, if they attempt that, are a routed host.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is strong.

Another group said: "there" refers to the protection of the idols and their support, that is, these people are a routed host in this path. Mujahid said: "there" refers to the Day of Badr, and it was an unseen matter which Allah informed of through His Messenger ﷺ, that the host of the polytheists would be defeated, so he went out at Badr. Another group said: it refers to those who were present in the year of the Trench in Medina. His saying: ﴿of the confederates﴾, that is, from among the total of the confederate nations who were zealous in falsehood and denied the messengers, so Allah the Exalted seized them.

The interpreters differed regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Dhi al-awtad﴾ [al-Fajr: 10]. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: he was so named because he had stakes and wooden pegs with which he played and upon which [people were tied]. Al-Suddi said: he used to kill people with the stakes, fastening them to the ground with them. Al-Dahhak said: he meant the great, enduring buildings. This is the most apparent of the sayings, just as mountains are called "stakes" for their firmness. It may also be said that "Dhi al-awtad" is an expression for the abundance of his tents and the greatness of his armies, and similar to this is their saying: "the people of the column" (ahl al-'amud). One group recited "Layka" and another group recited "al-Ayka," and this has been mentioned previously.

Then He, the Exalted, informed that these mentioned peoples are the confederates, and He set them as an example for Quraysh in that they denied, then He informed that His punishment is binding upon all of them; that is, likewise it is binding upon you, O deniers of Muhammad, peace be upon him. (p. 329) **"Yanzuru"** (ﷻ: *"yanẓuru"*) means *yantaẓiru* (awaits). This is a report from God Most High to His Messenger ﷺ, and reality has confirmed it. On this interpretation, *al-ṣayḥa* (the Cry) is an expression for everything that befell them of killing, captivity, and defeat, as when one says: "Time cried out against them." Qatada said: He threatened them with the Cry of the Resurrection and the blowing of the Trumpet. Al-Tha'labi said: This interpretation has been narrated as a *marfu'* report (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ). Another group said: He threatened them with a Cry by which they would be destroyed in this world. On both of these interpretations, the meaning of the speech is that they are on the path of punishment and under a grave matter, awaiting nothing but destruction. It does not mean a threat of a specific thing that Muhammad ﷺ awaits concerning them, as in the first interpretation.

Ṣ: **"Fawaq"** (ﷻ: *"fawāq"*) was read by the majority with an open *fa'* (*fawaq*). Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read it with a *ḍamma* on the *fa'* (*fuwaq*). Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Both have the same meaning, namely: it will have no cessation or return, but will continue until their destruction. From this comes *fawaq al-ḥalba* (the interval between two squirts of milk when milking), which is the pause between the two streams of milk. They also treated it like the interval between the cuts of hair. Among other things, there is the ḥadīth from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever stands guard for even the length of a milking interval, God forbids his body to the Fire." Ibn Zayd, Abu 'Ubayda, Mu'arrij, and al-Farra' said: The meaning differs. The *ḍamma* carries the sense mentioned above regarding *fawaq*, while the *fatḥa* means recovery, that is: after this Cry they will have no recovery or rest. Thus *fawaq* is like *jawāb*, from *ajāba* (to answer).

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned about them that they said: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our *qiṭṭ* before the Day of Reckoning﴾. *Al-qiṭṭ* means a portion or share. It also means a written decree or document from a ruler granting a gift or the like. From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

> *Nor the king al-Nu'man, on the day you meet him, in his prosperity,*
> *gives out the qutut (decrees) and bestows.*

It derives from *qaṭaṭtu*, meaning "I cut." People differed about what they meant by *al-qiṭṭ* here. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They meant, "Hasten for us our portion of good and blessing in our worldly life." Abu al-'Aliya and al-Kalbi said: They meant, "Hasten for us our records in our right hands," because when they heard in the Qur'an that the records will be given on the Day of Resurrection in the right or left hand, they said this. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: They meant the opposite of this, namely punishment and the like. This is the parallel to their saying: ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. Al-Suddi said: The meaning is, "Show us our dwellings in Paradise so that we may follow you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On every interpretation, their speech came in a manner of mockery and derision, and what is known of their disbelief, which persisted, indicates this. The wording of the verse nevertheless implies an acknowledgment of the Day of Reckoning.

As for God's saying: ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, that is, over these sayings by which they intend to mock, and do not pay attention to them. ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the one of might (*dha'l-ayd*)﴾, in religion and in proclaiming it. So follow his example and strengthen yourself as he was strengthened. *Al-ayd* means strength, and in Dawud's case it includes both bodily strength and strength in obedience. *Al-awwab* means one who returns repeatedly to obedience of God Most High. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said this, and al-Suddi explained it as "one who glorifies God." Al-Tha'labi mentioned that Abu Hurayra said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Blueness is blessing," and Dawud was blue-eyed. God, Blessed and Most High, informed us of the honour He bestowed upon Dawud, in that He subjected the mountains to glorify God along with him. The apparent meaning of the verse is the generality of mountains. Another group said: Rather, they are the mountains that were in his place and near him, and the glorification of the mountains here is literal. *Al-ishraq* is the time of the sun's brightness and its rising. From it comes their saying: "Shine forth, Thabir, so that we may raid," meaning: enter into the sunrise. At these two times was the prayer of the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: The *ḍuḥā* prayer among us is the prayer of *ishraq*, and it is referred to in this verse.

(p. 330) God's saying: ﴿And the birds﴾ is in conjunction with "the mountains," meaning: and We subjected the birds. *Maḥshūrah* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and its meaning is "gathered together." Ibn Abi 'Abla read *wa'l-ṭayru maḥshūratun* in the nominative in both places. As for the pronoun in *lahu* (to him), one group said it refers back to God Most High, so *kullun* is understood here to refer to Dawud, the mountains, and the birds. Other groups said it refers back to Dawud, peace be upon him, and *kullun* refers to the mountains and birds.

God, Most High, said: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾. This is a general expression for everything God Most High bestowed on him of strength, goodness, and blessing. Some exegetes specified certain things over others. Al-Suddi said: "With armies." Others said: "With a dignity that God Most High placed upon him." The majority read *wa-shadadnā* with the first *dāl* lightened, but it was narrated from al-Hasan that he read *shaddadnā* with the *dāl* doubled for emphasis. *Al-ḥikmah* (wisdom) means understanding in religion and soundness of judgment. This is the view of one group, while another group said that by *al-ḥikmah* is meant prophethood. Abu al-'Aliya said: *Al-ḥikmah* is knowledge that the intellects do not reject.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is the foundations of proof (*'aqā'id al-burhān*).

People differed about *faṣl al-khiṭāb* (decisive speech). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: It is the decisive judgment between people with truth, and hitting its target and understanding it. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, Shurayh, and al-Sha'bi said: It is requiring the oath from the defendant and the proof from the plaintiff. Ziyad and al-Sha'bi also said: It means the phrase "*amma ba'd*" (as for what follows), for he was the first to say it.

What the wording of the verse indicates is that God Most High gave him the ability that, whenever he addressed a matter, he explained the meaning, clarified it, and made it evident. Muhammad ﷺ surpasses this rank by conciseness of expression and by gathering many meanings into few words. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What the wording of the verse indicates is that God Most High gave him the ability that, whenever he addressed a matter, he explained the meaning, clarified it, and made it evident. No hesitation or weakness overtook him in this, and this is a quality that few attain. So his speech, peace be upon him, was decisive. God, Blessed and Most High, said concerning the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 13]. Muhammad ﷺ surpasses this rank by conciseness of expression and by gathering many meanings into few words. This is what he ﷺ was specially distinguished by, in his saying: "I have been given *jawāmi' al-kalim* (comprehensive words)," for these are among the qualities that no one before him was given. The mention of *jawāmi' al-kalim* is well-known and accepted for him ﷺ.

This is a commentary on Qur'an 38:21–24 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Has there come to you the news of the adversaries, when they climbed over the prayer niche?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed the bounds, and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Entrust it to me,' and he overcame me in speech.﴾ ﴿He said: 'He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe to add to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.' And Dawud realized that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down prostrating, and turned in repentance.﴾

This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it opens with a question, to express wonder at the story and to magnify it, because the meaning is: "Has there come to you this wondrous matter that is a lesson?" This interrogative is, in effect, preparing the addressee's soul and readying it to receive.

The word "al-khaṣm" (adversary), which functions like "ʿadl" and "zawr" (a noun used for the singular, dual and plural alike), is used for one, two, or many. From it is the verse of Labid:

"And an adversary who counts the blood-debts as if they were / Jealous lions, every bright one, a hardy one..."

This verse may allow that only two people climbed over the prayer niche, since the dispute itself was between two. In that case the pronouns in ﴿tasawwarū﴾ ("they climbed"), "dakhalū" ("they entered") and "qālū" ("they said") are used figuratively, expressing the two with a plural form. It may also allow that each party came with a companion acting as a supporter or companion, so that the term "adversary" applies to all of them, and the pronouns are then literal.

"Tasawwarū" means they climbed its wall. "Sūr" is the plural of "sūrah," which is a section of a building. This is like your saying: "I ascended the wall" or "the camel," when you climbed onto its hump. "Al-miḥrāb" is the highest place in a palace or a mosque, the place of worship. The governing word for the first "idh" (when) is "naba'" (news), and it has also been said to be "atāka" (has come to you). The governing word for the second "idh" is "tasawwarū." It has also been said that the second is a substitute (badal) for the first.

The words ﴿fa-faziʿa minhum﴾ ("and he was alarmed by them") may mean that his alarm was from the visitors themselves, lest they harm him, and he was alarmed because they entered not through the door and without seeking permission. It has been said that this occurred at night, as al-Tha'labi mentioned. It may also mean that his alarm was that the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them abandoned seeking permission, so his alarm was over the corruption of conduct, not from the visitors. The words "Do not fear" may indicate that they understood his alarm.

Here there is a story that people have elaborated at length, and the reports about it differ. It is necessary to mention only what the verse cannot be explained without. There is no disagreement among the exegetes that they were in fact angels, whom Allah sent as a parable for Dawud (peace be upon him). They brought the dispute to him concerning a matter in which he himself had fallen into something similar, and he gave a ruling that applied to his own case. When he perceived and understood the intent, he fell down, turned in repentance, and asked for forgiveness.

As for his own case into which he had fallen, it is reported that he (peace be upon him) sat in an assembly of the Children of Israel and was impressed by his own deeds, and there appeared from him something indicating that he did not fear for himself the trial. It is also said that a dialogue of this kind took place between him and the two guardian angels assigned to him, and he said: "Test me for a day, for although you are absent from me, I will not commit an abomination." Al-Suddi said: Dawud had divided his time: a day in which he judged between the people, a day for his worship, and a day for his own affairs. He was tried on the day when he was free for worship, when he wished to be given the like of the excellence of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub (peace be upon them), and he undertook to be tested as they had been tested. It has been said that other accounts of the cause exist, but they are lengthy and not authentic.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Dawud one day devoted himself to worship and withdrew into his prayer niche, praying and glorifying Allah, when a bird entered upon him through a window and landed before him. It is reported that it was a beautiful bird, a dove. Dawud stretched out his hand to take it, and it kept enticing him and he kept following it until it climbed up to the window through which it had entered. He climbed up to catch it, and the bird moved away from him. Dawud looked out and there he saw a woman bathing naked. He saw a beautiful sight, and it captivated him. Then she perceived him and let her hair fall over her body, covering herself with it, which increased his infatuation with her. Then he left and asked about her, and he was informed that she was the wife of a man from his army called Uriya, and that he was on such-and-such an expedition. It is reported that he wrote to the commander of that war to send this man forward to fight near the Ark, a place from which few escape. He was sent forward and was killed there. It is also reported that Dawud wrote that this man should be placed in command of a body of men and sent into raids and the most difficult fronts of the war, until he was killed in the third of his assaults. It is reported that Dawud had ninety-nine wives. When the letter came to him announcing the deaths of those killed in his war, he began to say, each time a man was named, "to Allah we belong and to Him we return," and he lamented. When the name of this man came, he said: "Death has been decreed upon every soul." Then he proposed to the woman and married her, and she was the mother of Sulayman (peace be upon him), as is reported from Qatada. So Allah sent to him the two adversaries to give a ruling that this was an injustice.

Another group said: all of this is what Dawud intended, but he did not do it, and the reproach was for the intention. Others said: the error was only that he did not grieve over the man as he grieved over other soldiers, since the matter of the woman was on his mind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The narrators of the first account are more numerous. In the books of the Children of Israel there are depictions of this story that are not fitting, and storytellers have related them in the context of this verse. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever relates what these storytellers have said about the matter of Dawud (peace be upon him), I will flog him two hadd punishments, for the violation he has committed against the sanctity of the one whom Allah has raised to a high station.

As for the words of Allah ﴿khaṣmān﴾ ("two adversaries," al-Ḥajj: 19), its implied meaning is: "We are two adversaries." This is like the saying of the poet:

"And say, when you have passed the land of ʿĀmir / and passed the two tribes of Nahd and Khathʿam,
'We are two strangers from Jurm ibn Zabbān, indeed they refused to give us provisions in time of hardship.'"

Similar to this is the Arab proverb "muḥsinatun fa-hīlī" ("you are good, so proceed"), where the implied meaning is "you are good." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Returning, repenting."

(p. 336) "Baghā" means to transgress and to act arrogantly. From it is the verse of the poet:

"But the youth Ḥamal ibn Badr / transgressed, and transgression's pasture is foul."

The words ﴿fa-ḥkum baynanā bil-ḥaqq wa-lā tushṭiṭ﴾ ("so judge between us with truth and do not exceed the bounds") are a rigorous address to the judge and a request for his justice, and this is not an expression of doubt on his part. From this is the saying of the man to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Judge between us by the Book of Allah." The majority read ﴿tushṭiṭ﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the first ṭā', meaning "do not transgress in your judgment." Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the first ṭā'; this is also the reading of al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī, and the meaning is "do not go far." One says "shaṭṭa" when something is far, and "ashaṭṭa" when one makes another go far. Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read "tushāṭiṭ" with a dammah on the tā' and an alif after the shīn. The phrase "sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ" means the middle of the road and its clear path.

As for the words ﴿innā hādhā akhī﴾ ("Indeed, this is my brother"), the grammatical status of "akhī" is an appositive ('aṭf bayān, explanatory apposition). The reason is that whatever among these qualifiers is a description, like creation, character and all other attributes, is a pure adjective (naʿt), and its governing word is the same as that of the thing described. Whatever among them cannot be used as a description at all is a substitute (badal), and its governing word is repeated. You say: "Your brother Zayd came to me," and the implied meaning is: "Your brother came to me, Zayd came to me," and the governing word is then omitted in both the substitute and the substituted noun, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ (Yā-Sīn: 31). Whatever among them cannot be used as a description, yet needs to be specified and serves the function of an adjective, is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān). This is clear in the verse of the poet:

"O Naṣr, victory, victory!"

For the reading of the second word with tanwīn indicates that the vocative is not repeated on it, so it is not a substitute, and the appositive is valid for it.

This brotherhood is a metaphor, since they were two angels, but insofar as they were imagined as two human beings, they spoke of the brotherhood that existed between them in religion and faith. And Allah knows best.

The word "naʿjah" (ewe) in this verse is used to express a woman. In the speech of the Arabs, "naʿjah" applies to a female wild cow and to a female sheep, and the Arabs also use it to express a woman, as they do with "shāh" (ewe). The poet al-A'sha said:

"So I shot, seizing the moment when his eye was distracted from his ewe, / and I hit the core of her heart and her spleen."

(p. 338) He meant: about his wife. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud there is "wa-tis'ūna naʿjatan unthā" ("and ninety-nine female ewes"). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "wa-liya" with a fatḥah on the yā', while the rest read it with sukūn; both are good. Al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj read "niʿjatan" with a kasrah on the nūn, while the majority have a fatḥah. Al-Ḥasan read "tis'un wa-tis'ūna" with a fatḥah on the tā' in both, and this is a dialect.

The words of Allah ﴿akfilnīhā﴾ mean: "Return it to my guardianship." Ibn Kaysān said: the meaning is "make it my portion (kifl)," that is, my share.

The words of Allah ﴿wa-ʿazzanī﴾ mean "he overcame me," and from it is the Arab saying: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," that is, whoever overcomes, takes spoil. (p. 339) Abu Ḥaywa read it with the zāy lightened. Abu al-Fatḥ said: he meant "ʿazzanī," and he dropped one of the two zāy's for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said:

"Ḥasan bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs"

Abu Ḥātim said: it was also narrated with the zāy lightened from ʿĀṣim. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Ḍuḥā and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wa-ʿāzzanī," meaning "he overpowered me." The meaning of the words ﴿fī al-khiṭāb﴾ ("in speech") is that he was more eloquent and stronger than I; when I address him, his speech is stronger than mine and his power greater than mine.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard this argument, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged it and was obstinate, so Dawud said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will break what is in your two eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ At that they both smiled, and they left and he did not see them at that moment. Then he realized the matter. It is reported that they departed toward the sky in plain view of him. It has also been said: rather they explained his act regarding that woman and her husband, and said to him: "We are only an example for you." Some people said: Dawud said ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ before he heard the other's argument, and this was his error, and this particular incident reported never befell him at all.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is weak in several respects, because it contradicts the widely transmitted reports. Also, the words ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ mean that your truthfulness became evident through evidence or confession, and this is part of the eloquence of the judge, by which he turns the crooked back to the truth and makes him understand the shrewdness that the judge possesses. al-Tha'labi said: in the case there was a confession from the defendant, which was omitted for brevity, and because of it Dawud (peace be upon him) said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾

(p. 340) As for the words of Allah (peace be upon him): ﴿by demanding your ewe,﴾ he attached the pronoun to the object. The "khulaṭāʾ" (associates) are partners and those who share in ownership and affairs in turn. This statement of Dawud is an admonition and an elaboration of a principle of truth, in order to warn against falling into what is contrary to the truth. The "mā" in the words ﴿and few are they﴾ is an emphatic redundant particle.

The words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ mean: he perceived and knew. Another group said: here "ẓanna" means "he was certain."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In the speech of the Arabs, "ẓann" in its essential meaning is always a hesitation between two beliefs, one of which prevails over the other, and the Arabs use it for knowledge that does not come through the senses and has no complete certainty at all. But people confuse this and say "ẓanna" means "he was certain." We do not find in the speech of the Arabs any evidence that supports saying: "Zayd saw such-and-such and so he thought it," and consider the words of Allah: ﴿So they thought that they were about to be overtaken by it﴾ (al-Kahf: 53), and the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

"So I said to them: 'Think that they are two thousand armored men, / their chiefs in the Persian coats of mail, woven and fitted.'"

And for this verse, ﴿"And David thought"﴾, you find that between it and certainty (yaqin) there is a degree. If we suppose that the people of the Fire had entered it and experienced it, one would not say "fa-zannu" (so they thought), and that would not be appropriate. And if Jibril had informed David of this trial, he would not have expressed it with "thanna (he thought)", for the Arabs use it only for knowledge that approaches certainty without being certainty. Had he not yet come to sensory experience?

The majority of readers recited ﴿"fatannahu" (We tested him)﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the nun, meaning: We tried him and examined him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, in one report from him, recited "fattannahu" with a shadda on the ta' and the nun, for the sense of intensification. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ali ibn Nasr, recited "fatanahu" with the ta' and nun lightened, on the basis that the verb belongs to the two litigants, meaning: they examined him concerning our command. This is the recitation of Qatadah. al-Dahhak recited "iftatanahu".

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿"and he fell down bowing and turned in repentance"﴾, means: he cast himself toward the ground, humbled and lowered. Ruku' (bowing) and sujud (prostration) both mean lowering oneself and inclining toward the ground, and the sacred law has specified them in known forms. Some said: one says "kharra thumma raka'a (he fell, then bowed)" even if he had not reached the ground. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is: he fell from his ruku', that is, he prostrated after having been in ruku'. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw myself writing Surat Sad, and when I reached this verse, the pen prostrated. And I saw myself in another dream, and a tree was reciting Sad, and when it reached this place it prostrated and said: 'O Allah, record for me by it a reward, remove from me by it a burden, grant me by it gratitude, and accept it from me as You accepted it from Your servant David.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'And you, Abu Sa'id, did you prostrate?' I said: No. He said: 'You were more deserving of prostration than the tree.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the verses until he reached ﴿"and turned in repentance"﴾, and prostrated, and said as the tree had said." "Anaba" means: he returned and repented.

It is narrated from Mujahid that David (peace be upon him) remained in that bowing, clinging to the ground, weeping and supplicating for forty mornings, until grass grew from his tears. Other reports have been related that are not established as sound. It is also related that when Allah forgave him the matter of the woman, he said: "O Lord, how shall I face the blood of her husband when he comes to seek me on the Day of Resurrection?" Allah revealed to him: "I shall ask him to grant it to you, O David, and I will make him willing to grant it, content with that." Then David (peace be upon him) was gladdened and his soul was at rest. It is related from 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Mujahid that David (peace be upon him) engraved his sin on his palm, so he would always see it and show it to the people at all times, in his sermons, speech, gestures and conduct, out of humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and as acknowledgment. He used to wander through the land crying out: "My God, when I remember my sin, the earth becomes narrow for me despite its vastness, and when I remember Your mercy, my spirit returns to me. Glory be to You, my God. I went to the physicians of religion to treat my illness, and they all directed me to You." He would begin his sermon with seeking forgiveness for the sinners, and he did not raise his head toward the sky after his sin, out of shame, until he died. May Allah, exalted is He, bless our Prophet and him, and all the prophets, and grant them peace.

You say: "Your brother Zayd came to me," and the implied meaning is: "Your brother came to me, Zayd came to me," and the governing word is then omitted in both the substitute and the substituted noun, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ (Yā-Sīn: 31). Whatever among them cannot be used as a description, yet needs to be specified and serves the function of an adjective, is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān). This is clear in the verse of the poet:

"O Naṣr, victory, victory!"

For the reading of the second word with tanwīn indicates that the vocative is not repeated on it, so it is not a substitute, and the appositive is valid for it.

This brotherhood is a metaphor, since they were two angels, but insofar as they were imagined as two human beings, they spoke of the brotherhood that existed between them in religion and faith. And Allah knows best.

The word "naʿjah" (ewe) in this verse is used to express a woman. In the speech of the Arabs, "naʿjah" applies to a female wild cow and to a female sheep, and the Arabs also use it to express a woman, as they do with "shāh" (ewe). The poet al-A'sha said:

"So I shot, seizing the moment when his eye was distracted from his ewe, / and I hit the core of her heart and her spleen."

(p. 338) He meant: about his wife. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud there is "wa-tis'ūna naʿjatan unthā" ("and ninety-nine female ewes"). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "wa-liya" with a fatḥah on the yā', while the rest read it with sukūn; both are good. Al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj read "niʿjatan" with a kasrah on the nūn, while the majority have a fatḥah. Al-Ḥasan read "tis'un wa-tis'ūna" with a fatḥah on the tā' in both, and this is a dialect.

The words of Allah ﴿akfilnīhā﴾ mean: "Return it to my guardianship." Ibn Kaysān said: the meaning is "make it my portion (kifl)," that is, my share.

The words of Allah ﴿wa-ʿazzanī﴾ mean "he overcame me," and from it is the Arab saying: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," that is, whoever overcomes, takes spoil. (p. 339) Abu Ḥaywa read it with the zāy lightened. Abu al-Fatḥ said: he meant "ʿazzanī," and he dropped one of the two zāy's for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said:

"Ḥasan bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs"

Abu Ḥātim said: it was also narrated with the zāy lightened from ʿĀṣim. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Ḍuḥā and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wa-ʿāzzanī," meaning "he overpowered me." The meaning of the words ﴿fī al-khiṭāb﴾ ("in speech") is that he was more eloquent and stronger than I; when I address him, his speech is stronger than mine and his power greater than mine.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard this argument, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged it and was obstinate, so Dawud said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will break what is in your two eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ At that they both smiled, and they left and he did not see them at that moment. Then he realized the matter. It is reported that they departed toward the sky in plain view of him. It has also been said: rather they explained his act regarding that woman and her husband, and said to him: "We are only an example for you." Some people said: Dawud said ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ before he heard the other's argument, and this was his error, and this particular incident reported never befell him at all.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is weak in several respects, because it contradicts the widely transmitted reports. Also, the words ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ mean that your truthfulness became evident through evidence or confession, and this is part of the eloquence of the judge, by which he turns the crooked back to the truth and makes him understand the shrewdness that the judge possesses. al-Tha'labi said: in the case there was a confession from the defendant, which was omitted for brevity, and because of it Dawud (peace be upon him) said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾

(p. 340) As for the words of Allah (peace be upon him): ﴿by demanding your ewe,﴾ he attached the pronoun to the object. The "khulaṭāʾ" (associates) are partners and those who share in ownership and affairs in turn. This statement of Dawud is an admonition and an elaboration of a principle of truth, in order to warn against falling into what is contrary to the truth. The "mā" in the words ﴿and few are they﴾ is an emphatic redundant particle.

The words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ mean: he perceived and knew. Another group said: here "ẓanna" means "he was certain."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In the speech of the Arabs, "ẓann" in its essential meaning is always a hesitation between two beliefs, one of which prevails over the other, and the Arabs use it for knowledge that does not come through the senses and has no complete certainty at all. But people confuse this and say "ẓanna" means "he was certain." We do not find in the speech of the Arabs any evidence that supports saying: "Zayd saw such-and-such and so he thought it," and consider the words of Allah: ﴿So they thought that they were about to be overtaken by it﴾ (al-Kahf: 53), and the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

"So I said to them: 'Think that they are two thousand armored men, / their chiefs in the Persian coats of mail, woven and fitted.'"

And for this verse, ﴿"And David thought"﴾, you find that between it and certainty (yaqin) there is a degree. If we suppose that the people of the Fire had entered it and experienced it, one would not say "fa-zannu" (so they thought), and that would not be appropriate. And if Jibril had informed David of this trial, he would not have expressed it with "thanna (he thought)", for the Arabs use it only for knowledge that approaches certainty without being certainty. Had he not yet come to sensory experience?

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, in one report from him, recited "fattannahu" with a shadda on the ta' and the nun, for the sense of intensification. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ali ibn Nasr, recited "fatanahu" with the ta' and nun lightened, on the basis that the verb belongs to the two litigants, meaning: they examined him concerning our command. This is the recitation of Qatadah. al-Dahhak recited "iftatanahu".

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿"and he fell down bowing and turned in repentance"﴾, means: he cast himself toward the ground, humbled and lowered. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw myself writing Surat Sad, and when I reached this verse, the pen prostrated. And I saw myself in another dream, and a tree was reciting Sad, and when it reached this place it prostrated and said: 'O Allah, record for me by it a reward, remove from me by it a burden, grant me by it gratitude, and accept it from me as You accepted it from Your servant David.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'And you, Abu Sa'id, did you prostrate?' I said: No. He said: 'You were more deserving of prostration than the tree.' Glory be to You, my God. I went to the physicians of religion to treat my illness, and they all directed me to You." He would begin his sermon with seeking forgiveness for the sinners, and he did not raise his head toward the sky after his sin, out of shame, until he died. May Allah, exalted is He, bless our Prophet and him, and all the prophets, and grant them peace.

This is a commentary on Qur'an 38:21–24 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Has there come to you the news of the adversaries, when they climbed over the prayer niche?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed the bounds, and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Entrust it to me,' and he overcame me in speech.﴾ ﴿He said: 'He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe to add to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.' And Dawud realized that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down prostrating, and turned in repentance.﴾

This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it opens with a question, to express wonder at the story and to magnify it, because the meaning is: "Has there come to you this wondrous matter that is a lesson?" This interrogative is, in effect, preparing the addressee's soul and readying it to receive.

The word "al-khaṣm" (adversary), which functions like "ʿadl" and "zawr" (a noun used for the singular, dual and plural alike), is used for one, two, or many. From it is the verse of Labid:

"And an adversary who counts the blood-debts as if they were / Jealous lions, every bright one, a hardy one..."

This verse may allow that only two people climbed over the prayer niche, since the dispute itself was between two. In that case the pronouns in ﴿tasawwarū﴾ ("they climbed"), "dakhalū" ("they entered") and "qālū" ("they said") are used figuratively, expressing the two with a plural form. It may also allow that each party came with a companion acting as a supporter or companion, so that the term "adversary" applies to all of them, and the pronouns are then literal.

"Tasawwarū" means they climbed its wall. "Sūr" is the plural of "sūrah," which is a section of a building. This is like your saying: "I ascended the wall" or "the camel," when you climbed onto its hump. "Al-miḥrāb" is the highest place in a palace or a mosque, the place of worship. The governing word for the first "idh" (when) is "naba'" (news), and it has also been said to be "atāka" (has come to you). The governing word for the second "idh" is "tasawwarū." It has also been said that the second is a substitute (badal) for the first.

The words ﴿fa-faziʿa minhum﴾ ("and he was alarmed by them") may mean that his alarm was from the visitors themselves, lest they harm him, and he was alarmed because they entered not through the door and without seeking permission. It has been said that this occurred at night, as al-Tha'labi mentioned. It may also mean that his alarm was that the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them abandoned seeking permission, so his alarm was over the corruption of conduct, not from the visitors. The words "Do not fear" may indicate that they understood his alarm.

Here there is a story that people have elaborated at length, and the reports about it differ. It is necessary to mention only what the verse cannot be explained without. There is no disagreement among the exegetes that they were in fact angels, whom Allah sent as a parable for Dawud (peace be upon him). They brought the dispute to him concerning a matter in which he himself had fallen into something similar, and he gave a ruling that applied to his own case. When he perceived and understood the intent, he fell down, turned in repentance, and asked for forgiveness.

As for his own case into which he had fallen, it is reported that he (peace be upon him) sat in an assembly of the Children of Israel and was impressed by his own deeds, and there appeared from him something indicating that he did not fear for himself the trial. It is also said that a dialogue of this kind took place between him and the two guardian angels assigned to him, and he said: "Test me for a day, for although you are absent from me, I will not commit an abomination." Al-Suddi said: Dawud had divided his time: a day in which he judged between the people, a day for his worship, and a day for his own affairs. He was tried on the day when he was free for worship, when he wished to be given the like of the excellence of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub (peace be upon them), and he undertook to be tested as they had been tested. It has been said that other accounts of the cause exist, but they are lengthy and not authentic.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Dawud one day devoted himself to worship and withdrew into his prayer niche, praying and glorifying Allah, when a bird entered upon him through a window and landed before him. It is reported that it was a beautiful bird, a dove. Dawud stretched out his hand to take it, and it kept enticing him and he kept following it until it climbed up to the window through which it had entered. He climbed up to catch it, and the bird moved away from him. Dawud looked out and there he saw a woman bathing naked. He saw a beautiful sight, and it captivated him. Then she perceived him and let her hair fall over her body, covering herself with it, which increased his infatuation with her. Then he left and asked about her, and he was informed that she was the wife of a man from his army called Uriya, and that he was on such-and-such an expedition. It is reported that he wrote to the commander of that war to send this man forward to fight near the Ark, a place from which few escape. He was sent forward and was killed there. It is also reported that Dawud wrote that this man should be placed in command of a body of men and sent into raids and the most difficult fronts of the war, until he was killed in the third of his assaults. It is reported that Dawud had ninety-nine wives. When the letter came to him announcing the deaths of those killed in his war, he began to say, each time a man was named, "to Allah we belong and to Him we return," and he lamented. When the name of this man came, he said: "Death has been decreed upon every soul." Then he proposed to the woman and married her, and she was the mother of Sulayman (peace be upon him), as is reported from Qatada. So Allah sent to him the two adversaries to give a ruling that this was an injustice.

Another group said: all of this is what Dawud intended, but he did not do it, and the reproach was for the intention. Others said: the error was only that he did not grieve over the man as he grieved over other soldiers, since the matter of the woman was on his mind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The narrators of the first account are more numerous. In the books of the Children of Israel there are depictions of this story that are not fitting, and storytellers have related them in the context of this verse. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever relates what these storytellers have said about the matter of Dawud (peace be upon him), I will flog him two hadd punishments, for the violation he has committed against the sanctity of the one whom Allah has raised to a high station.

As for the words of Allah ﴿khaṣmān﴾ ("two adversaries," al-Ḥajj: 19), its implied meaning is: "We are two adversaries." This is like the saying of the poet:

"And say, when you have passed the land of ʿĀmir / and passed the two tribes of Nahd and Khathʿam,
'We are two strangers from Jurm ibn Zabbān, indeed they refused to give us provisions in time of hardship.'"

Similar to this is the Arab proverb "muḥsinatun fa-hīlī" ("you are good, so proceed"), where the implied meaning is "you are good." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Returning, repenting."

(p. 336) "Baghā" means to transgress and to act arrogantly. From it is the verse of the poet:

"But the youth Ḥamal ibn Badr / transgressed, and transgression's pasture is foul."

The words ﴿fa-ḥkum baynanā bil-ḥaqq wa-lā tushṭiṭ﴾ ("so judge between us with truth and do not exceed the bounds") are a rigorous address to the judge and a request for his justice, and this is not an expression of doubt on his part.
