This is a commentary on Qur'an 38:21–24 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Has there come to you the news of the adversaries, when they climbed over the prayer niche?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed the bounds, and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Entrust it to me,' and he overcame me in speech.﴾ ﴿He said: 'He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe to add to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they.' And Dawud realized that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down prostrating, and turned in repentance.﴾

This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it opens with a question, to express wonder at the story and to magnify it, because the meaning is: "Has there come to you this wondrous matter that is a lesson?" This interrogative is, in effect, preparing the addressee's soul and readying it to receive.

The word "al-khaṣm" (adversary), which functions like "ʿadl" and "zawr" (a noun used for the singular, dual and plural alike), is used for one, two, or many. From it is the verse of Labid:

"And an adversary who counts the blood-debts as if they were / Jealous lions, every bright one, a hardy one..."

This verse may allow that only two people climbed over the prayer niche, since the dispute itself was between two. In that case the pronouns in ﴿tasawwarū﴾ ("they climbed"), "dakhalū" ("they entered") and "qālū" ("they said") are used figuratively, expressing the two with a plural form. It may also allow that each party came with a companion acting as a supporter or companion, so that the term "adversary" applies to all of them, and the pronouns are then literal.

"Tasawwarū" means they climbed its wall. "Sūr" is the plural of "sūrah," which is a section of a building. This is like your saying: "I ascended the wall" or "the camel," when you climbed onto its hump. "Al-miḥrāb" is the highest place in a palace or a mosque, the place of worship. The governing word for the first "idh" (when) is "naba'" (news), and it has also been said to be "atāka" (has come to you). The governing word for the second "idh" is "tasawwarū." It has also been said that the second is a substitute (badal) for the first.

The words ﴿fa-faziʿa minhum﴾ ("and he was alarmed by them") may mean that his alarm was from the visitors themselves, lest they harm him, and he was alarmed because they entered not through the door and without seeking permission. It has been said that this occurred at night, as al-Tha'labi mentioned. It may also mean that his alarm was that the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them abandoned seeking permission, so his alarm was over the corruption of conduct, not from the visitors. The words "Do not fear" may indicate that they understood his alarm.

Here there is a story that people have elaborated at length, and the reports about it differ. It is necessary to mention only what the verse cannot be explained without. There is no disagreement among the exegetes that they were in fact angels, whom Allah sent as a parable for Dawud (peace be upon him). They brought the dispute to him concerning a matter in which he himself had fallen into something similar, and he gave a ruling that applied to his own case. When he perceived and understood the intent, he fell down, turned in repentance, and asked for forgiveness.

As for his own case into which he had fallen, it is reported that he (peace be upon him) sat in an assembly of the Children of Israel and was impressed by his own deeds, and there appeared from him something indicating that he did not fear for himself the trial. It is also said that a dialogue of this kind took place between him and the two guardian angels assigned to him, and he said: "Test me for a day, for although you are absent from me, I will not commit an abomination." Al-Suddi said: Dawud had divided his time: a day in which he judged between the people, a day for his worship, and a day for his own affairs. He was tried on the day when he was free for worship, when he wished to be given the like of the excellence of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub (peace be upon them), and he undertook to be tested as they had been tested. It has been said that other accounts of the cause exist, but they are lengthy and not authentic.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Dawud one day devoted himself to worship and withdrew into his prayer niche, praying and glorifying Allah, when a bird entered upon him through a window and landed before him. It is reported that it was a beautiful bird, a dove. Dawud stretched out his hand to take it, and it kept enticing him and he kept following it until it climbed up to the window through which it had entered. He climbed up to catch it, and the bird moved away from him. Dawud looked out and there he saw a woman bathing naked. He saw a beautiful sight, and it captivated him. Then she perceived him and let her hair fall over her body, covering herself with it, which increased his infatuation with her. Then he left and asked about her, and he was informed that she was the wife of a man from his army called Uriya, and that he was on such-and-such an expedition. It is reported that he wrote to the commander of that war to send this man forward to fight near the Ark, a place from which few escape. He was sent forward and was killed there. It is also reported that Dawud wrote that this man should be placed in command of a body of men and sent into raids and the most difficult fronts of the war, until he was killed in the third of his assaults. It is reported that Dawud had ninety-nine wives. When the letter came to him announcing the deaths of those killed in his war, he began to say, each time a man was named, "to Allah we belong and to Him we return," and he lamented. When the name of this man came, he said: "Death has been decreed upon every soul." Then he proposed to the woman and married her, and she was the mother of Sulayman (peace be upon him), as is reported from Qatada. So Allah sent to him the two adversaries to give a ruling that this was an injustice.

Another group said: all of this is what Dawud intended, but he did not do it, and the reproach was for the intention. Others said: the error was only that he did not grieve over the man as he grieved over other soldiers, since the matter of the woman was on his mind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The narrators of the first account are more numerous. In the books of the Children of Israel there are depictions of this story that are not fitting, and storytellers have related them in the context of this verse. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever relates what these storytellers have said about the matter of Dawud (peace be upon him), I will flog him two hadd punishments, for the violation he has committed against the sanctity of the one whom Allah has raised to a high station.

As for the words of Allah ﴿khaṣmān﴾ ("two adversaries," al-Ḥajj: 19), its implied meaning is: "We are two adversaries." This is like the saying of the poet:

"And say, when you have passed the land of ʿĀmir / and passed the two tribes of Nahd and Khathʿam,
'We are two strangers from Jurm ibn Zabbān, indeed they refused to give us provisions in time of hardship.'"

Similar to this is the Arab proverb "muḥsinatun fa-hīlī" ("you are good, so proceed"), where the implied meaning is "you are good." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Returning, repenting."

(p. 336) "Baghā" means to transgress and to act arrogantly. From it is the verse of the poet:

"But the youth Ḥamal ibn Badr / transgressed, and transgression's pasture is foul."

The words ﴿fa-ḥkum baynanā bil-ḥaqq wa-lā tushṭiṭ﴾ ("so judge between us with truth and do not exceed the bounds") are a rigorous address to the judge and a request for his justice, and this is not an expression of doubt on his part. From this is the saying of the man to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Judge between us by the Book of Allah." The majority read ﴿tushṭiṭ﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the first ṭā', meaning "do not transgress in your judgment." Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the first ṭā'; this is also the reading of al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī, and the meaning is "do not go far." One says "shaṭṭa" when something is far, and "ashaṭṭa" when one makes another go far. Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read "tushāṭiṭ" with a dammah on the tā' and an alif after the shīn. The phrase "sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ" means the middle of the road and its clear path.

As for the words ﴿innā hādhā akhī﴾ ("Indeed, this is my brother"), the grammatical status of "akhī" is an appositive ('aṭf bayān, explanatory apposition). The reason is that whatever among these qualifiers is a description, like creation, character and all other attributes, is a pure adjective (naʿt), and its governing word is the same as that of the thing described. Whatever among them cannot be used as a description at all is a substitute (badal), and its governing word is repeated. You say: "Your brother Zayd came to me," and the implied meaning is: "Your brother came to me, Zayd came to me," and the governing word is then omitted in both the substitute and the substituted noun, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ (Yā-Sīn: 31). Whatever among them cannot be used as a description, yet needs to be specified and serves the function of an adjective, is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān). This is clear in the verse of the poet:

"O Naṣr, victory, victory!"

For the reading of the second word with tanwīn indicates that the vocative is not repeated on it, so it is not a substitute, and the appositive is valid for it.

This brotherhood is a metaphor, since they were two angels, but insofar as they were imagined as two human beings, they spoke of the brotherhood that existed between them in religion and faith. And Allah knows best.

The word "naʿjah" (ewe) in this verse is used to express a woman. In the speech of the Arabs, "naʿjah" applies to a female wild cow and to a female sheep, and the Arabs also use it to express a woman, as they do with "shāh" (ewe). The poet al-A'sha said:

"So I shot, seizing the moment when his eye was distracted from his ewe, / and I hit the core of her heart and her spleen."

(p. 338) He meant: about his wife. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud there is "wa-tis'ūna naʿjatan unthā" ("and ninety-nine female ewes"). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "wa-liya" with a fatḥah on the yā', while the rest read it with sukūn; both are good. Al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj read "niʿjatan" with a kasrah on the nūn, while the majority have a fatḥah. Al-Ḥasan read "tis'un wa-tis'ūna" with a fatḥah on the tā' in both, and this is a dialect.

The words of Allah ﴿akfilnīhā﴾ mean: "Return it to my guardianship." Ibn Kaysān said: the meaning is "make it my portion (kifl)," that is, my share.

The words of Allah ﴿wa-ʿazzanī﴾ mean "he overcame me," and from it is the Arab saying: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," that is, whoever overcomes, takes spoil. (p. 339) Abu Ḥaywa read it with the zāy lightened. Abu al-Fatḥ said: he meant "ʿazzanī," and he dropped one of the two zāy's for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said:

"Ḥasan bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs"

Abu Ḥātim said: it was also narrated with the zāy lightened from ʿĀṣim. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Ḍuḥā and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wa-ʿāzzanī," meaning "he overpowered me." The meaning of the words ﴿fī al-khiṭāb﴾ ("in speech") is that he was more eloquent and stronger than I; when I address him, his speech is stronger than mine and his power greater than mine.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard this argument, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged it and was obstinate, so Dawud said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will break what is in your two eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ At that they both smiled, and they left and he did not see them at that moment. Then he realized the matter. It is reported that they departed toward the sky in plain view of him. It has also been said: rather they explained his act regarding that woman and her husband, and said to him: "We are only an example for you." Some people said: Dawud said ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ before he heard the other's argument, and this was his error, and this particular incident reported never befell him at all.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is weak in several respects, because it contradicts the widely transmitted reports. Also, the words ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾ mean that your truthfulness became evident through evidence or confession, and this is part of the eloquence of the judge, by which he turns the crooked back to the truth and makes him understand the shrewdness that the judge possesses. al-Tha'labi said: in the case there was a confession from the defendant, which was omitted for brevity, and because of it Dawud (peace be upon him) said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾

(p. 340) As for the words of Allah (peace be upon him): ﴿by demanding your ewe,﴾ he attached the pronoun to the object. The "khulaṭāʾ" (associates) are partners and those who share in ownership and affairs in turn. This statement of Dawud is an admonition and an elaboration of a principle of truth, in order to warn against falling into what is contrary to the truth. The "mā" in the words ﴿and few are they﴾ is an emphatic redundant particle.

The words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ mean: he perceived and knew. Another group said: here "ẓanna" means "he was certain."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In the speech of the Arabs, "ẓann" in its essential meaning is always a hesitation between two beliefs, one of which prevails over the other, and the Arabs use it for knowledge that does not come through the senses and has no complete certainty at all. But people confuse this and say "ẓanna" means "he was certain." We do not find in the speech of the Arabs any evidence that supports saying: "Zayd saw such-and-such and so he thought it," and consider the words of Allah: ﴿So they thought that they were about to be overtaken by it﴾ (al-Kahf: 53), and the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

"So I said to them: 'Think that they are two thousand armored men, / their chiefs in the Persian coats of mail, woven and fitted.'"

And for this verse, ﴿"And David thought"﴾, you find that between it and certainty (yaqin) there is a degree. If we suppose that the people of the Fire had entered it and experienced it, one would not say "fa-zannu" (so they thought), and that would not be appropriate. And if Jibril had informed David of this trial, he would not have expressed it with "thanna (he thought)", for the Arabs use it only for knowledge that approaches certainty without being certainty. Had he not yet come to sensory experience?

The majority of readers recited ﴿"fatannahu" (We tested him)﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the nun, meaning: We tried him and examined him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, in one report from him, recited "fattannahu" with a shadda on the ta' and the nun, for the sense of intensification. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ali ibn Nasr, recited "fatanahu" with the ta' and nun lightened, on the basis that the verb belongs to the two litigants, meaning: they examined him concerning our command. This is the recitation of Qatadah. al-Dahhak recited "iftatanahu".

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿"and he fell down bowing and turned in repentance"﴾, means: he cast himself toward the ground, humbled and lowered. Ruku' (bowing) and sujud (prostration) both mean lowering oneself and inclining toward the ground, and the sacred law has specified them in known forms. Some said: one says "kharra thumma raka'a (he fell, then bowed)" even if he had not reached the ground. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is: he fell from his ruku', that is, he prostrated after having been in ruku'. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw myself writing Surat Sad, and when I reached this verse, the pen prostrated. And I saw myself in another dream, and a tree was reciting Sad, and when it reached this place it prostrated and said: 'O Allah, record for me by it a reward, remove from me by it a burden, grant me by it gratitude, and accept it from me as You accepted it from Your servant David.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'And you, Abu Sa'id, did you prostrate?' I said: No. He said: 'You were more deserving of prostration than the tree.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the verses until he reached ﴿"and turned in repentance"﴾, and prostrated, and said as the tree had said." "Anaba" means: he returned and repented.

It is narrated from Mujahid that David (peace be upon him) remained in that bowing, clinging to the ground, weeping and supplicating for forty mornings, until grass grew from his tears. Other reports have been related that are not established as sound. It is also related that when Allah forgave him the matter of the woman, he said: "O Lord, how shall I face the blood of her husband when he comes to seek me on the Day of Resurrection?" Allah revealed to him: "I shall ask him to grant it to you, O David, and I will make him willing to grant it, content with that." Then David (peace be upon him) was gladdened and his soul was at rest. It is related from 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Mujahid that David (peace be upon him) engraved his sin on his palm, so he would always see it and show it to the people at all times, in his sermons, speech, gestures and conduct, out of humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and as acknowledgment. He used to wander through the land crying out: "My God, when I remember my sin, the earth becomes narrow for me despite its vastness, and when I remember Your mercy, my spirit returns to me. Glory be to You, my God. I went to the physicians of religion to treat my illness, and they all directed me to You." He would begin his sermon with seeking forgiveness for the sinners, and he did not raise his head toward the sky after his sin, out of shame, until he died. May Allah, exalted is He, bless our Prophet and him, and all the prophets, and grant them peace.

[p. 341] [p. 342]

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verse 25–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿So We forgave him that. And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return.﴾ ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Account.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ ﴿[This is] a Book We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ means: We covered it up. "That" refers to the earlier sin. "Al-zulfa" means nearness and a lofty station. "Al-ma'ab" means the place of return in the Hereafter, from: "aba ya'ub" when he returned. After this there is an ellipsis indicated by the apparent meaning of the speech, its estimation being: And We said to him: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah﴾. Some people derived from this verse that the earth requires a khalifah from Allah, may He be exalted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not necessarily implied by the verse; rather its necessity comes from the Shari'ah and the consensus (ijma' – scholarly agreement). It is not said "khalifat Allah" (Caliph of Allah) except for His Messenger. As for the caliphs, each one of them is the khalifah of the one before him. What comes in poetry of calling one of them "khalifat Allah" is an exaggeration and excess, as Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*"The khalifah of Allah over His creation, the pens and the books have dried up by that."*

Do you not see that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, clarified this meaning, so they said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq:

(p-343) "Khalifat Rasul Allah (Successor of the Messenger of Allah)." Thus he was called by this during his term. When 'Umar took over, they said: "Ya khalifata khalifat Rasul Allah (O successor of the successor of the Messenger of Allah)," but the matter became long, and they saw that in the future it would become much longer, so they called him: "Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Believers)," and this title remained restricted to the caliphs.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ is an interjection between the two statements concerning the matter of Dawud and Sulayman. It is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ) and an admonition to his ummah, and a warning to the disbelievers in him. Abu Haywah recited: "yudillun" with a damma on the ya'. "Nasu" in this verse means: they abandoned.

Allah, may He be exalted, informed that those who disbelieve assume that the creation of the heaven and the earth and what is between them is mere falsehood with no meaning, and that the matter does not lead to reward or punishment. Allah, may He be exalted, informed of the falsity of their assumption and threatened them with the Fire. Then He, may He be exalted, stated the distinction – in His view – between the believers who do righteous deeds and the corrupting disbelievers, and between the righteous and the wicked. In this statement there is encouragement to faith and an incitement to it, and a warning to the disbelievers.

Then He referred the seeking of faith and piety to His Mighty Book by His saying: ﴿A Book﴾, meaning: this is a Book for whoever wishes to hold fast to faith and to nearness to Us. In these verses there is a brief and wondrous concision, like the inimitability of the Mighty Qur'an. He described it as blessed because it gathers all blessing in it: for it bequeaths Paradise, rescues from the Fire, protects a person in the life of this world, and becomes the cause of the elevation of his rank in the life of the Hereafter. The majority read ﴿liyaddabbaru﴾ with a ya', with the doubling of the dal and the ba', and the pronoun refers to the people of the world. Hafs from 'Asim read "litaddabbaru" with a ta', in the second-person address. Abu Bakr [from 'Asim] read it with the dal lightened; its origin is "tatadabbaru." The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that reflection (tadabbur) is among the reasons for the revelation of the Qur'an, so recitation in measured manner (tartil) is better for this, since reflection does not occur except with measured recitation. The rest of the verse is clear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 38, verses 30–35:**

(p-344) God, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And We gave to David, Solomon, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who often turned (to God).﴾ ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening, the poised, swift steeds.﴾ ﴿He said: "I have loved the love of good (things) over the remembrance of my Lord," until they were hidden behind the veil.﴾ ﴿"Bring them back to me," so he began passing his hand over their shins and necks.﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned (to God) in repentance.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾

Hibah (gift) and 'atiyyah (bestowal) have the same meaning. God granted Solomon to David as a son, and God, exalted is He, praised him with attributes of commendation, contained in His saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The word awwab means rajja' (one who returns often). The word ﴿awwab﴾ is the governing element (al-'amil) of idh ("when"), because the matter of the horses requires a great returning.

People differed about the account of these displayed horses. The majority said that thousands of horses were displayed before Solomon, peace be upon him, which his father had left to him. It was also said that they were a single thousand, and they were made to run before him in the evening. He became absorbed in their beauty, their running, and his love for them, until he missed the time of the evening prayer. Qatadah said it was the afternoon prayer, and similar is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He regretted this, and said: "Bring the horses back to me." Al-Hasan said: "So he began striking their necks and hamstrings with the sword, slaughtering them because they had been the cause of missing the prayer." So Allah replaced them for him with something swifter than them, the wind. A group of people, among them al-Tha'labi, said: "There was a famine among the people, and the flesh of horses was lawful to them. He slaughtered them only so that they might be eaten, as a means of drawing near to God through them, like the hadyu (sacrificial offering) among us." Similar to this is what Abu Talhah al-Ansari did with his garden, when he gave it in charity after the dabsi (a kind of fly/insect) entered upon him during prayer and distracted him.

Al-ṣāfin (the poised one, a technical term for a horse): the horse that raises one of its forelegs and stands on the tip of its hoof; it may also do this with a hind leg, and it is a sign of nobility of breed. Al-Zajjaj recited:

*He has become accustomed to standing poised, and he never stops, as if, from what stands on three legs, he is broken.*

(p-345) Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-ṣāfin is the one who gathers its two forelegs together and levels them. As for the one that stands on the tip of the hoof, it is al-mukhayyam. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, it reads: "al-ṣawafin al-jiyad" (the poised, the swift). Al-jiyad is the plural of jawd, like thawb and thiyab, and it was named so because it is generous (yajud) with its running.

Some people said: "Al-khayr" here means horses, and the Arabs call horses "khayr." Likewise, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to Zayd al-Khayl: "You are Zayd of Goodness (Zayd al-Khayr)." And ḥubba is the object (maf'ul bihi) of "aḥbabtu," placed in the accusative according to a group, as if "aḥbabtu" means "preferred." Another group said: the object of "aḥbabtu" is omitted, and ḥubba is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "I loved these horses with the love of good (things)." In this interpretation, "al-khayr" is other than the horses. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "ḥubba al-khayli," with the lam. Another group said: "aḥbabtu" means: I fell to the ground because of my sin, derived from "aḥabba al-ba'ir" when the camel became exhausted and fell down from thinness. According to this, ḥubba is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

The pronoun in "tawarat" (it was hidden) refers to the sun, even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, since the meaning requires it to be understood as mentioned and implied; and because al-'ashiy (evening) requires a reference to it, as it is estimated and imagined in relation to it. Some commentators said regarding this verse, "until they were hidden behind the veil": it means the horses, i.e., they entered their stables.

(p-346) Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zahrawi said that his passing his hand over their shins and necks was not with the sword, but with his hand, honoring and loving them. Al-Tabari preferred this. Some said: rather, it was washing with water, and mash (wiping) may be used for washing, because wiping with the hands accompanies it. In my view, these statements are only based on a certain kind of interpretation of this verse, and it has been reported from some people. That is because he saw that this account involved no missing of a prayer, and did not include a matter of horses returning or coming back. So the governing element in "idh" is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember when there was displayed." They said: the horses were displayed to Solomon while he was in prayer, so he gestured to them, meaning "I am in prayer," and they removed them from him until they brought them into the stables. He said, when he had finished his prayer: "I have loved the love of good," i.e., that which is with God in the Hereafter, because of the remembrance of my Lord. It is as if he were saying: "That distracted me from seeing the horses until they were brought into their stables. Bring them back to me," so he began passing his hand over their necks and shins out of love for them.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned that this wiping was only a marking on the shins and necks, with a mark of confinement in the way of God, exalted is He. Most people hold that they were inherited horses. Some said: he slew them until no more than one hundred horses remained of them, and from the offspring of those hundred comes every horse that exists today. This is far-fetched. Some said: they were horses which the devils (shayatin) brought out for him from the sea, and they had wings. It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were twenty horses. "Tafiqa" means: he continued doing, as you say: "ja'ala yaf'alu" (he began to do).

The majority read ﴿bi-l-sūq﴾ with a silent waw. It is the plural of saq (shin). Ibn Kathir alone read it with a hamza. Abu 'Ali said: it is weak, but its justification by analogy is that since the damma came adjacent to the waw, it was estimated to be on it, so it was hamzated, as they do with a damma-ed waw. This is similar to their inclination of the alif of miqlat, since the qaf came adjacent to the kasra, so they estimated that the qaf was the one with the kasra.

(p-347) The justification for the hamza of "al-sūq" from transmitted usage is that Abu Hayyah al-Numayri used to hamzate every silent waw preceded by a damma, and he would recite:

*"Al-mu'qidan" have loved Musa to you.*

Ibn Muhaysin read: "bi-l-su'uq," with a hamza followed by a waw. And His saying ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ — under every interpretation, "'an" here indicates passing from one thing to another. So reflect on it, for it is consistent.

Then God, exalted is He, informed about His testing of Solomon and his trial, for the loss of his kingdom. It is reported regarding this that one of Solomon's favored wives said to him: "My brother has a dispute, so I would like you to decide for him in such-and-such a way," for something other than the truth. Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "I will do it." So God punished him (p-348) by setting a jinn over his ring. That is because Solomon, peace be upon him, would not enter the lavatory with the ring of sovereignty, out of reverence for the name of God, exalted is He. So he would place it with one of his wives. He did that one day, so God cast his likeness upon a jinn named Sakhr, according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It was also said other than this, which we have omitted because it is not authentic. So he came to the woman, and she handed him the ring. He took control of Solomon's kingdom, and remained in it for forty days. He threw Solomon's ring into the sea, and began to act wrongly among the Children of Israel, with Solomon's likeness, until they denied his deeds. God empowered him over all the kingdom. Mujahid said: except over Solomon's wives, for he did not uncover them. During that time, Solomon, peace be upon him, had gone out fleeing in the direction of his face, unrecognized, and he would not claim kinship to any people without being struck by them. Hunger and destitution overtook him. One day he passed by a woman who was washing a dead fish, so he asked her for some of it because of his hunger. It was said: rather, he bought it, and she gave him two fish. He began to open their bellies, and in the belly of one of them was his ring. So his kingdom returned to him, and the jinn and the wind were subjected to him from that day. Sakhr the jinn fled, so Solomon gave orders about him, and he was brought to him. He covered him with stones and imprisoned him in the sea until the Day of Resurrection. This is the trial with which Solomon, peace be upon him, was tested and examined.

People differed about the body that was cast upon his throne. The majority said it was the aforementioned jinn, and he called it "a body" because it had taken the form of Solomon's body while not being him. This is the most sound of the sayings and the clearest in meaning. A group said: rather, it was the body of a dead son of his that was cast upon his throne. Another group said: rather, it was the half of the child who was born to him when he swore that he would go around to his wives, and did not make an exception in his oath. Some people said: Solomon, peace be upon him, became ill with an illness like fainting, until he was upon his throne as one without a soul.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is not connected to the meaning of this verse.

God's saying ﴿anab﴾ (he turned in repentance) means: he desisted, turned back, and responded to obedience to his Lord. The meaning of this is: from that lapse by which the trial came about.

Then Solomon, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for forgiveness, and asked Him to bestow a kingdom. The interpreters differed (p-349) about the meaning of His saying ﴿that is not fitting for anyone after me﴾. The majority said: he meant that He should single him out among mankind, so that it would be specific to him and an honor. This is the apparent meaning of the statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the report about the ifrit who confronted him during his prayer, and he seized him intending to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque. He said: "Then I remembered the saying of my brother Solomon: 'My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after me,' so I released him." Qatadah and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: Solomon, peace be upon him, meant only: "It is not fitting for anyone after me during my lifetime," i.e., I will not be deprived of it, and it will not pass to anyone as it passed to the jinn.

It is reported in the defamations of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf that when he recited this verse, he said: "He was indeed envious." This is one of al-Hajjaj's wickednesses. Solomon, peace be upon him, is certainly to be understood as having intended by that a righteous, permissible aim, because a person may desire from the bounty of God that which no one else attains, especially according to the standing of prophethood. Consider His saying, peace be upon him: ﴿"it is not fitting"﴾; it is a word that carries possibility and is not a certainty that God does not give the like of that kingdom to anyone. And Muhammad, ﷺ, if he had tied the jinn, would not have been a deficiency, since it would not have been what was given to Solomon, peace be upon him. But because there was some resemblance in it, he left it, out of his own choice, always preferring the easier of the two matters and the nearer of the two to humility, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running gently by his command, wherever he directed﴾ ﴿and the devils, every builder and diver﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains﴾ ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account﴾ ﴿and indeed for him is nearness with Us and a good return﴾

Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "al-riyah" (the winds, in the plural), while the majority read it in the singular. God Almighty subjected the wind to Sulayman, peace be upon him. He had a great throne (kursi), said to carry four thousand horsemen, and it is also said more. Upon it were the devils, and birds shaded him, and there came upon him a violent wind (i'sar), which lifted it from the earth until it reached the air; then the gentle wind (al-rakha') took hold of it. The rakha' is the soft yet strong wind, uniform, not bringing violent gusts, so that it carries him; its morning journey is a month and its evening journey is a month. The phrase ﴿wherever he directed﴾ means "wherever he intended," as Wahb and others said. Al-Tha'labi recited:

"He hit the speech but could not manage, so he missed the answer at the joint."

It is likely that "aṣāba" here is transitive, from ṣāba yaṣūbu, meaning: wherever he directed his armies and made them pour down like the pouring of clouds and rain. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "he intended," and likewise your saying to the speaker "aṣabta" means "you intended the truth."

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the devils." The meaning is: everyone who built his fortresses for wars. "Muqarrinin" means bound, with some of them tied to others. "Al-asfad" means shackles and fetters.

People differed regarding what is referred to by His saying ﴿This is Our gift﴾. Qatadah said: it is a reference to what he did with the jinn: bestow upon whom you wish of them, release him from his bonds and dismiss him from his service, or withhold his affair as you wish. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it refers to what He granted him of women and empowered him to have intercourse with them. Al-Hasan said: it refers to all the dominion He gave him, and commanded him to bestow upon whom he wills and withhold from whom he wills. It is as though He placed him under a limit regarding the measure of the blessing, then permitted him to dispose of it by his own will, while He, Exalted, knew of him that his will would only be exercised in accordance with obedience to Allah. This is the most correct of the opinions and the most comprehensive for explaining the verse. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verses 41–44:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And remember Our servant Job, when he called out to his Lord, "Surely Satan has touched me with hardship and suffering."﴾ ﴿"Strike with your foot. This is a cool bath and a drink."﴾ ﴿And We gave him back his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding.﴾ ﴿And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it, and do not break your oath. Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one who turned back (to Allah) often.﴾

Job (Ayyub) was a prophet from the Children of Israel, from the descendants of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). He was tested in his body, his wealth and his family, while his belief and his religion remained sound.

It is related concerning this that Allah empowered Satan over him in order to tempt him away from his religion. So he afflicted him in his wealth and said to him, "If you obey me, your wealth will return." He did not obey him. Then he afflicted him in his family and his children, and they all perished, and Satan said to him, "If you had obeyed me, they would have returned." He did not obey him. Then he afflicted his body, and Job remained steadfast in obedience to Allah's command for seven years and seven months. This is what Qatada said. Anas related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Job (peace be upon him) remained in his trial for eighteen years, his flesh falling away, until people grew weary of him, and no one remained patient with him except his wife."

It is also related that the cause for which Allah tested him was that he entered upon some of the kings, saw an evil (munkar) and did not change it. It is also related that the cause was that he slaughtered a sheep and had it cooked, and it was eaten in his presence while his neighbour was hungry, and he did not give him any of it. It is also related that when Job's affliction and patience reached their extreme, two men passed by him, men with whom he had some acquaintance. They reproached him and said to him, "You have committed a sin no one has committed like it." He understood from them a mockery directed at him, and at that point he supplicated and called out to his Lord.

As for his saying (peace be upon him), ﴿Satan has touched me﴾, it may refer to the touch (of Satan) when Allah empowered him over him, as we have mentioned. It may also mean his touch of him from the beginning, when he drove him to commit the sin because of which the trial came, either by leaving off changing the evil in the presence of the king, or by leaving off comforting the neighbour. It was said that he referred to Satan's touch of him in approaching his family and asking him to associate partners with Allah. Job had complained about this act, and it was more severe upon him than his illness.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أنِّي﴾ (annī) with a fatḥa on the hamza. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a kasra. It is in a position of naṣb (accusative) through the omission of the preposition. The majority of reciters read ﴿"بِنُصْبٍ"﴾ (bi-nuṣbin) with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. Hubayra, from Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with a fatḥa on the nūn, and this is the reading of al-Jahdari and Ya'qub, and it is related from al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far. Abu 'Umara, from Hafs, from 'Asim, read "بِنُصُبٍ" (bi-nuṣubin) with a ḍamma on both the nūn and the ṣād, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and al-Hasan, according to one report from him. Hubayra also related from Hafs, from 'Asim, a reading with a fatḥa on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. All of these have one meaning, namely hardship. The word "النَصَبُ" (al-naṣab) is often used for the hardship of fatigue. Some people distinguished between these forms, but the correct view is that they are dialectal variants from the expression "أنْصَبَنِي الأمْرُ وَنَصَبَنِي" (the matter made me weary and exhausted me), meaning when it was difficult for me. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Weariness from Umayma has wearied you, a source of toil."

And from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Leave me to my grief, O Umayma, one who is wearied."

The Qāḍī Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It has been said concerning this verse that "nāṣib" means "munṣib", and that it is in the nisba form (the relative form), meaning "one possessing toil."

There is much that is omitted in this verse, and its implied meaning is: So Allah responded to him and said to him, ﴿"Strike with your foot"﴾. Rakḍ (ركض) means striking with the foot, and the meaning is: strike the ground. It is related from Qatada that this command was in al-Jabiya in the land of Syria. It is also related that Job (peace be upon him) was commanded to strike the ground, so he struck it, and a clear, cool spring of water gushed forth for him. He drank from it, and every illness within his body departed, then he washed himself, and what was on the outside of his body departed. It is also related that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him: he drank from one and washed in the other.

Nāfi', Shayba, 'Asim and al-A'mash read ﴿"وَعَذابٌ ارْكُضْ"﴾ with a ḍamma on the nūn of the tanwīn. The majority of the reciters of Basra read it with a kasra. "Mughtasal" (مُغْتَسَلٌ) means a place of washing, or water for washing, just as you say, "this matter is considered (mu'tabar)" and "this water is a place of washing (mughtasal)" in the same way.

It is related that Allah the Exalted gave him back his family and his wealth in this world, returned those among them who had died, restored what had perished of his livestock and property, then blessed all of that, and children were born to him until his affairs multiplied. It is also related that all of this is a promise for the Hereafter, meaning that Allah will do this for him in the Hereafter. The first view is more common among the exegetes. ﴿"Mercy"﴾ (raḥmatan) is in the accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun) of cause. The words of the Exalted, ﴿"and a reminder" (wa dhikrā)﴾, mean an admonition and a reminder by which people of intellect take lesson, and take example from his patience in hardships, and never despair of Allah's mercy in any state.

It is also related that during the period of his illness, Job's wife would go to him, and Satan would meet her in the form of a physician, and at other times in the form of an advisor, and in other forms. He would say to her, "If this sick man prostrated to such-and-such an idol, he would be cured. If he slaughtered a female goat for such-and-such an idol, he would be cured," and he would present to her aspects of disbelief. She would sometimes present that to Job, and he would say to her, "Have you let the enemy of Allah into your path?" When she angered him with this and similar things, he swore to her that if he recovered from his illness, he would strike her one hundred lashes. When he recovered, Allah commanded him to take a ḍighth (ضِغْث) containing one hundred twigs. The ḍighth is a large handful of rods or similar wet branches, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk and the lexicographers. He was to strike her with it one blow, and thus his oath would be fulfilled. From this is the expression, "ḍighth 'alā ibāla" (a bundle upon a bundle), where the ibāla is a bundle of firewood. The poet said:

"Below me is a plump she-camel that I have tied up, and I have thrown down a bundle of fragrant bitter herbs."

This is a ruling that has also come in our Sharia from the Prophet (ﷺ), similar to it in the case of a man who was disabled and committed fornication. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded a palm branch containing one hundred shoots, or something close to that, and he was struck with it once. Abu Dawud related the hadith. Some of the jurists of the Ummah have held this view. Mālik and his companions do not hold this view, and most scholars likewise reject saying it, and hold that the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) and the fulfilment of oaths (birr fī al-aymān) occur only with the complete number of strikes.

It is also related that the cause was that he slaughtered a sheep and had it cooked, and it was eaten in his presence while his neighbour was hungry, and he did not give him any of it. It is also related that when Job's affliction and patience reached their extreme, two men passed by him, men with whom he had some acquaintance. They reproached him and said to him, "You have committed a sin no one has committed like it." He understood from them a mockery directed at him, and at that point he supplicated and called out to his Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verse 45–54:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, possessors of strength and vision.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾ ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and excellent.﴾ ﴿And remember Ishmael, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl, and each is among the excellent.﴾ ﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is a good return.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, whose doors are opened for them.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, of equal age.﴾ ﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no exhaustion.﴾

Ibn Kathir recited: "wa-dhkur ʿabdanā" (in the singular), and this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the people of Makkah. The rest recited: ﴿wa-dhkur ʿibādanā﴾ (in the plural). According to this reading, the three entered both the remembrance and the servitude. As for the reading of the one who recites "ʿabdanā", Makki and others said: they entered the remembrance, but they did not enter the servitude except through another verse. There is scrutiny in this. Some of the interpreters took from this verse that the one sacrificed was Isaac, from the fact that Allah the Exalted mentioned him right after mentioning Job, prophets whom He tested with trials as He tested Job, and He did not mention Ishmael because he was among those who were not tested.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak.

The majority recited: ﴿"ulī al-aydī"﴾, and al-Hasan, al-Thaqafi, al-A'mash and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "ulī al-ayd" with the omission of the yā'. As for "ulū", it is the plural of "dhū" (possessor). As for the first reading, "al-aydī" in it is an expression for strength in obedience to Allah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. A group said: rather, its meaning is: possessors of hands and bounties which Allah bestowed upon them: of prophethood and station. Some said: the meaning is: the hands of the limbs, and what is meant is the hands that act in goodness, and the eyes (al-abṣār) that are piercing in it, unlike those that are neglected in most people. As for the one who recited "al-ayd" without a yā', it is possible that it is like the one with the yā' and it was dropped for lightness; and since the alif and lām substitute for tanwīn (nunation), it is required that it be dropped along with them as it is dropped with tanwīn. A group said: "al-ayd" means strength, and what is meant is obedience to Allah the Exalted. His saying the Exalted: ﴿"wa-l-abṣār"﴾ is an expression for insights, i.e., they see the realities and look with the light of Allah the Exalted; and with this similar meaning all have interpreted.

Nafi' alone recited: "bi-khāliṣati dhikrā" with idafa (construct), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Shayba. The rest recited: ﴿"bi-khāliṣatin dhikrā"﴾ with tanwīn. al-A'mash recited: "bi-khāliṣatihim dhikrā", and this is the reading of Talha. It is possible that "khāliṣa" is an active participle, as if it expressed a distinction or a rank. As for the one who put it in idafa, "dhikrā" is genitive by the idafa; as for the one who used tanwīn, "dhikrā" is a substitute (badal) for "khāliṣa". It is possible that "khāliṣa" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like "al-ʿāfiya" and "khā'inat al-aʿyun" and others, so "dhikrā" on this basis is either in the accusative position by the verbal noun, on the estimate: "Indeed We purified them by purifying for them the remembrance of the Abode", and "khāliṣa" is a verbal noun from "akhlaṣa", with the augmentations dropped; or "dhikrā" is in the nominative position by the verbal noun, on the estimate: "Indeed We purified them by the remembrance of the Abode becoming pure for them", and "khāliṣa" is from "khalaṣa". And "al-dār" in every case is in the accusative position governed by "dhikrā", and "dhikrā" is a verbal noun. The verse may intend by "al-dār" the Abode of the Hereafter, in the sense: We purified them by the reminder of the Hereafter becoming pure for them, and calling people to it and urging them toward it; this is the saying of Qatada. Or in the sense: their remembrance of the Hereafter and their fear of it became pure for them, and acting accordingly; this is the saying of Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: We bestowed upon them the best of what is in the Hereafter, purified them with it, and gave it to them. It is possible that it intends by "al-dār" the abode of this world, in the sense of mention of praise and exaltation from people, and the lasting commendation which is the eternity by which one is recompensed; so the verse comes in the sense of His saying the Exalted: ﴿"a tongue of truthfulness"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84], and in the sense of His saying: ﴿"And We left for him among later generations"﴾ [al-Saffat: 108].

"al-Mustafayn" its origin is "al-mustafayīn": the yā' moved and what preceded it was fatḥa, so it changed into an alif; then the sukun of the alif and the sukun of the yā' which is the sign of the plural met, so the alif was dropped. "al-Akhyar" is the plural of "khayr", and "khayr" is a lightened form of "khayyir", like "mayt" and "mayyit".

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-l-yasaʿa", as if he had introduced the definite article onto "yasaʿa", treating it as "ḍaygham" and the like; this is the reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and of the Kufans. The rest recited: "wa-l-yasaʿa". Abu ʿAli said: the alif and lām in it are extra and not definite, as they are in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I picked for you truffles and ʿasāqil,
And indeed I forbade you from the daughters of al-awbar."

"Banat al-awbar" is a kind of truffle. There was disagreement regarding the prophethood of (Dhul-Kifl), and the explanation of his matter has already preceded.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿"hādhā dhikr"﴾ may carry two meanings: one of them is that it refers to the praise of those mentioned and the preservation of honour for them, and so this interpretation supports the saying of whoever said earlier that "al-dār" is meant as the worldly abode; the second is that it refers by "this" to the Qur'an, i.e., it is a reminder for the world. "Al-ma'āb" is the place of return where they return. "Jannāt" is a substitute for "ḥusn", "mufattaḥa" is an adjective for "jannāt", and "al-abwāb" is a grammatically unnamed subject (naʾib al-fāʿil, passive); the estimate according to the Kufans is: "mufattiḥa lahum abwābuhā" (its doors opened for them), and this is not permitted according to the people of Basra; the estimate according to them is: "al-abwāb minhā" (the doors of it). What prompted this pronoun is that an adjective must have a returning pronoun referring back to the described noun.

As for ﴿qāṣirāt al-ṭarf﴾, Qatada said: its meaning is: restricting their gaze to their husbands. "Atrāb" means peers, and its origin among the sons of Adam is that their ages are one, i.e., their bodies touched the dust at one time. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited "yūʿadūn" with the yā' from below, and they differed regarding the sura of Qaf; Abu ʿAmr recited it with the tā' from above, and the rest recited in both surahs with the tā'. "Al-nafād" is the perishing and ending.

Ibn Kathir recited: "wa-dhkur ʿabdanā" (in the singular), and this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the people of Makkah. The rest recited: ﴿wa-dhkur ʿibādanā﴾ (in the plural). According to this reading, the three entered both the remembrance and the servitude. As for the reading of the one who recites "ʿabdanā", Makki and others said: they entered the remembrance, but they did not enter the servitude except through another verse. There is scrutiny in this. Some of the interpreters took from this verse that the one sacrificed was Isaac, from the fact that Allah the Exalted mentioned him right after mentioning Job, prophets whom He tested with trials as He tested Job, and He did not mention Ishmael because he was among those who were not tested.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak.

The majority recited: ﴿"ulī al-aydī"﴾, and al-Hasan, al-Thaqafi, al-A'mash and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "ulī al-ayd" with the omission of the yā'. As for "ulū", it is the plural of "dhū" (possessor). As for the first reading, "al-aydī" in it is an expression for strength in obedience to Allah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. A group said: rather, its meaning is: possessors of hands and bounties which Allah bestowed upon them: of prophethood and station. Some said: the meaning is: the hands of the limbs, and what is meant is the hands that act in goodness, and the eyes (al-abṣār) that are piercing in it, unlike those that are neglected in most people. As for the one who recited "al-ayd" without a yā', it is possible that it is like the one with the yā' and it was dropped for lightness; and since the alif and lām substitute for tanwīn (nunation), it is required that it be dropped along with them as it is dropped with tanwīn. A group said: "al-ayd" means strength, and what is meant is obedience to Allah the Exalted. His saying the Exalted: ﴿"wa-l-abṣār"﴾ is an expression for insights, i.e., they see the realities and look with the light of Allah the Exalted; and with this similar meaning all have interpreted.

Nafi' alone recited: "bi-khāliṣati dhikrā" with idafa (construct), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Shayba. The rest recited: ﴿"bi-khāliṣatin dhikrā"﴾ with tanwīn. al-A'mash recited: "bi-khāliṣatihim dhikrā", and this is the reading of Talha. It is possible that "khāliṣa" is an active participle, as if it expressed a distinction or a rank. As for the one who put it in idafa, "dhikrā" is genitive by the idafa; as for the one who used tanwīn, "dhikrā" is a substitute (badal) for "khāliṣa". **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 38, verses 55–61:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿This is so. And for the transgressors is an evil place of return.﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in; how wretched a resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾ ﴿And other punishments of its kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you. No welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say: "Rather, it is you. No welcome for you. You brought this upon us, so how wretched is the abode."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase his punishment double in the Fire."﴾

The estimated reading (al-taqdir) is: "The matter is this." It is also possible that the estimate is: "This is what occurs," or something similar. "Al-taghi" means one who is excessive in evil, derived from "taghā yatghā." Here, "al-tughyan" refers to disbelief. "Al-ma'ab" means the place of return. "Jahannam" is a substitute (badal, apposition) for the phrase ﴿an evil place of return﴾. The phrase ﴿yaslawnaha﴾ means they directly experience its heat and burning. "Al-mihad" is what a person spreads out and makes use of.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿This, so let them taste it﴾ may be understood in several ways. "Hadha" may be the inchoative (mubtada', subject), with "hamim" as its predicate (khabar). It may also be that the estimate is: "The matter is this, so let them taste it." Or "hadha" may be in the accusative position governed by a verb implied by ﴿so let them taste it﴾, and then "hamim" is, according to this, the predicate of an implied subject. Ibn Zayd said: "Al-hamim is their tears, which collect in basins, and then they are made to drink them." Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿wa-ghassaq﴾ with a light (takhfif) sin. It is a noun meaning "that which flows." It is narrated from Qatadah that it is what flows from the pus of the people of the Fire. It is narrated from al-Suddi that it is what flows from their eyes. It is narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that it is what flows from the venom of the scorpions of the Fire, which, it is said, are gathered in a certain pit there. Al-Dahhak said: "It is the coldest of things." 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah said: "It is the most foul-smelling of things," and Abu Sa'id narrated this from the Prophet (ﷺ). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿wa-ghassaq﴾ with a doubled sin, meaning "flowing." This is the reading of Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Wthab, and Talhah. The meaning of it, according to what we have mentioned of the differences, is the same, but this reading is weak (qira'at du'f), because ﴿ghassaq﴾ is either an adjective, in which case the verse would require the omission of the qualified noun and the placing of the adjective in its position, which is not preferable here; or it is a noun, and nouns of this pattern are few in the speech of the Arabs, such as "al-qayyad" and similar words.

The majority of people read ﴿wa-akhar﴾ in the singular. It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'). Its predicate has been disputed. One group said its estimate is: "And for them is another punishment." Another group said its predicate is ﴿azwaj﴾ (pairs). The phrase ﴿min shaklihi﴾ means that the whole, which is "pairs," is predicated of the one, insofar as that one comprises degrees and ranks of punishment, some intense and some less so. Also, from another perspective, each part of that may be called by the name of the whole, as they say: "his parting (mafriq) has turned gray," so they make each part of the parting a parting. And as they say: "a camel with dewlaps." Do you not see that a number of the exegetes said that this other punishment is the zamharir (extreme cold)? It is as if they made each part of it a zamharir. Abu 'Amr alone read ﴿wa-ukhar﴾ in the plural. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Isa. It is in the nominative as a subject, its predicate is ﴿azwaj﴾, and ﴿min shaklihi﴾ is in the position of an adjective (sifah). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, as did Abu Hatim, because the adjective is plural. The word ﴿ukhar﴾ is not declined (lam yansarif) because it is a form deviated (ma'dul) from the definite article used as an adjective. The principle of "af'al" and its plural is that it should not be used except with the definite article, so when "ukhar" is used without the definite article, this is a deviation from that rule. It is permissible for "ukhar" to be described by an indefinite noun, as in His saying: ﴿fa-'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. This differs from all [p-359] words deviated from the definite article, such as "saḥar" and similar, in that it is not permissible for an indefinite noun to be described by them. This deviation in "ukhar" is counted in preventing its declension, but it is not counted in preventing it from describing an indefinite noun, just as they count a thing in one ruling and not in another, like the "lam" in their saying: "la abā laka" (no father to you), and the "lam" attached to the "kaf" is counted as a separator for the genitive construction (idafah), which is why "la" was permitted to enter, but it was not counted in that "aba" was declined by means of a particle, while its nature, when it is separate and not annexed, is to be declined by the vowel-signs. So the "lam" came with its ruling cancelled, insofar as "aba" is declined by vowels as if it were annexed, and it is counted as a separator in that it permitted the entry of "la." Mujahid read ﴿min shiklihi﴾ with a kasra on the shin. The word ﴿azwaj﴾ means "kinds." The meaning is: for them are hamim and ghassaq, and other foods of the same type as what has been mentioned, and many kinds.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿This is a troop﴾ refers to what is said to the people of the Fire when the general body of disbelievers and their followers are driven in, because their leaders enter the Fire first. The more apparent view is that the one who says this to them is the angels of punishment, and this is what al-Tha'labi and others related. It is possible that this is said by some of them to others, so the other group says: ﴿No welcome for them﴾, meaning: no spaciousness of place and no good will they meet. "Al-fawj" is a group of people. His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Rather, it is you. No welcome for you﴾ is a report of the saying of the followers when they heard the saying of the leaders. ﴿You brought this upon us﴾ means: by your misguidance you sent ahead for us what necessitated this, so it is as if you did this to us.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿They say: "Our Lord"﴾ is also a report of the saying of the followers, who call down against their leaders that their punishment be doubled.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 38, verses 55–61:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿This is so. And for the transgressors is an evil place of return.﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in; how wretched a resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾ ﴿And other punishments of its kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you. No welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say: "Rather, it is you. No welcome for you. "Al-taghi" means one who is excessive in evil, derived from "taghā yatghā." Here, "al-tughyan" refers to disbelief. "Al-ma'ab" means the place of return. "Jahannam" is a substitute (badal, apposition) for the phrase ﴿an evil place of return﴾. The phrase ﴿yaslawnaha﴾ means they directly experience its heat and burning. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verses 62–66:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And they will say, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the evil?"﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes swung away from them?﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no god except Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving."﴾

The pronoun in "they will say" refers to the leaders and chiefs of the disbelievers. Allah informs that they will remember, when they enter the Fire, a group of the weak among the believers, and so they will say this statement. This is consistent in every nation to which a messenger came. It is narrated that the disbelievers of the time of the Prophet ﷺ who made this statement were Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Umayya ibn Khalaf, the people of the well (al-qalib), and those who followed their course. It is also narrated that the men to whom they point by mention are 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb and their like; this was said by Mujahid and others. The meaning is: in the world we used to count them as evil, having no good portion.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i inclined the rā' of "al-ashrar" (imala, a pronunciation in which the vowel is raised toward i); Ibn Kathir and 'Asim pronounced it with a fatha; Nafi' used ishmam (a partial rounding of the vowel); and Hamza pronounced it [in the same manner].

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "attakhadhnahum" with a connecting alif (hamzat wasl), and its meaning is that this would be in the position of a description of "rijal" (men). The rest read it with a cutting alif (hamzat qat') as an interrogative, and its meaning is a self-reproach of themselves upon this, in the manner of rebuke to it and regret, i.e., "Did we take them as objects of mockery, when they were not such?" Abu 'Ali found the meaning of this reading unlikely.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "sukhriyyan" with a dammah on the sin, which is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba, Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Abu Ja'far, Mujahid and al-Dahhak; its meaning is from "sukhra" (servitude) and "istikhdam" (employment). The rest read it with a kasrah on the sin, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Isa and Ibn Muhaysin; its well-known meaning is from "sakhar", which is mockery, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, news has come to me, by which I am not gladdened, from 'Alw, which is neither a lie nor mockery (sakhar)."

A group said: the kasrah of the sin may be from "taskhir" (subjugation).

The "am" in their saying, "Or have our eyes swung away from them?" is equivalent (mu'adilah) to the "ma" in their saying, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see?" This is because it may be equivalent to what is equivalent to "man." Some grammarians denied this and said that it is only equivalent to the alif alone. The estimate in this verse is: "Are they missing from us, or have [our eyes] swung away?" The meaning of this speech is: "Are they not with us, or are they with us, but our eyes swing away from them so that we do not see them?" And "al-zaygh" is inclination.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, informed His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire.﴾ "Dispute" is a substitute (badal) for His saying "is true." Ibn Abi 'Abla read "takhasumu" with a fatha on the mim, Ibn Muhaysin read "takhasumun" with tanwin, and "ahli al-nar" with a damma on the lam.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to be free for the disbelievers from all aims except that he is a warner to them. This is an eloquent threat that stirs souls. The rest of the verse is clear.

Abu 'Ali found the meaning of this reading unlikely.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "sukhriyyan" with a dammah on the sin, which is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba, Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Abu Ja'far, Mujahid and al-Dahhak; its meaning is from "sukhra" (servitude) and "istikhdam" (employment). The rest read it with a kasrah on the sin, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Isa and Ibn Muhaysin; its well-known meaning is from "sakhar", which is mockery, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, news has come to me, by which I am not gladdened, from 'Alw, which is neither a lie nor mockery (sakhar)."

A group said: the kasrah of the sin may be from "taskhir" (subjugation).

The "am" in their saying, "Or have our eyes swung away from them?" is equivalent (mu'adilah) to the "ma" in their saying, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see?" This is because it may be equivalent to what is equivalent to "man." Some grammarians denied this and said that it is only equivalent to the alif alone. The estimate in this verse is: "Are they missing from us, or have [our eyes] swung away?" The meaning of this speech is: "Are they not with us, or are they with us, but our eyes swing away from them so that we do not see them?" And "al-zaygh" is inclination.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, informed His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire.﴾ "Dispute" is a substitute (badal) for His saying "is true." Ibn Abi 'Abla read "takhasumu" with a fatha on the mim, Ibn Muhaysin read "takhasumun" with tanwin, and "ahli al-nar" with a damma on the lam.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to be free for the disbelievers from all aims except that he is a warner to them. This is an eloquent threat that stirs souls. The rest of the verse is clear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 38, verses 67–74:**

The Exalted said:

﴿Say, "It is a great news."﴾ ﴿You turn away from it.﴾ ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed.﴾ ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner.﴾ ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely,﴾ ﴿except Iblis. He was arrogant and was among the disbelievers.﴾

The reference in the Exalted's words ﴿Say, "It is a great news."﴾ is to tawhid (the oneness of God) and the return (al-ma'ad). It refers to the Qur'an and everything it contains, and to His promise that belief in it is salvation and denial of it is destruction. Al-Tabari transmitted that a Bedouin (a'rabi) brought a dispute before Shurayh, and [the Bedouin] testified against him. Shurayh wanted to enforce the judgment, but the Bedouin said, "Are you judging against me by the news?" Shurayh said, "Yes. Indeed God, exalted is He, says: ﴿It is a great news,﴾" and he recited the verse and gave judgment against him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This answer from Shurayh was only according to the wording of the Bedouin, and he did not clarify the matter with him. He was only aiming at what would settle it for him, because the Bedouin did not distinguish between testimony (shahada) and news (naba'), and "al-naba'" in the language of the Arabs means "report" (khabar). Then the Exalted rebuked them with His words: ﴿You turn away from it.﴾ Then He said: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed,﴾ and this is an argument for the validity of the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. It is as if He says: This is a weighty matter, and you turn away from it despite its validity. The proof of its validity is that I inform you in it of unseen matters that could come only from God, for I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their dispute, were it not that God, exalted is He, informed me of that. By the "Assembly" He meant the angels. The pronoun in ﴿they dispute﴾ according to the majority of the exegetes refers to the angels.

People differed about the matter over which their dispute was. One group said: their dispute was about the affair of Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring, regarding placing them on earth, and what the verses that follow indicate supports this. So the angels' words ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ [al-Baqara: 30] are the dispute. Another group said: rather, their dispute was about expiations (kaffarat), forgiveness of sins, and the like. When a servant does a good deed, the angels differ about the measure of its reward, until God decides as He wills. A hadith has come regarding this which Ibn Fawrak explained, because it contains: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that his Lord, mighty and majestic, said to him in his sleep: 'What do they dispute about?' I said: 'I do not know.' He said: 'About the expiations, which are: completing the ablution in difficult conditions, walking to the congregations,' the hadith in full, [and he] said: 'Then God, glorified and exalted, placed His hand between my shoulders until I found its coolness between my breasts.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The interpretation of this hadith is that the hand is the blessing of knowledge. His saying ﷺ "its coolness" (bardaha) means the joy in it and the comfort (thalj), as the Arabs say about a pleasant matter: "How cool it is upon the liver!" and the like. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ [p-363]: "Prayer at night is the cool spoil (al-ghanima al-barida)," meaning the easy gain with which a person is gladdened.

Another group said: what is meant by ﴿the Exalted Assembly﴾ is the angels, and the Exalted's words ﴿when they dispute﴾ are cut off from it, meaning: when the disbelieving Arabs dispute about the Exalted Assembly, some of them say they are the daughters of God, and some of them say they are deities who are worshipped, and other than that of their sayings.

Another group said: by "the Exalted Assembly" He meant the Quraysh. This is a weak view that is not strengthened from any direction.

Most people recited ﴿"that indeed"﴾ with a fatha on the alif, as if He is saying: "Only the warning," whereas Abu Ja'far recited "illa innama" (only indeed) as a reported speech (hikaya), as if it was said to him: "You are a clear warner," and so he related the meaning. This is like when a person says, "Am I knowledgeable?" and it is said to him, "You are knowledgeable," and so he relates the meaning.

The ﴿when﴾ in the Exalted's words ﴿when your Lord said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿when﴾, according to the interpretation of one who sees the dispute as concerning who will be appointed on earth. According to the other views, the operator (al-'amil) of the second ﴿when﴾ is an implied verb, its estimate being: "And remember when He said." The "created human" is Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿I proportioned him﴾ means his person. ﴿I breathed into him﴾ is an expression for causing the spirit to pass into him, an expression in line with what is understood from things being caused by breath. The Exalted's words ﴿of My spirit﴾ are an idafa of ownership to the owner, because all spirits belong to God, blessed and exalted is He, and He attributed it to Himself as an honour. Regarding the Exalted's words ﴿prostrating﴾, people differed: one group said it is the known prostration, and another group said it means "humbling oneself" (khadi'in), based on the original meaning of prostration in the language. Then the Exalted informed that the angels, by His command, prostrated, except Iblis, for he was arrogant toward prostrating.

The Exalted's words ﴿and was among the disbelievers﴾ may mean: he was among the disbelievers from the beginning of his affair in God's knowledge, exalted is He. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said. And it may mean: he was found, at this moment of heedlessness, to be among the disbelievers. According to both views, God has judged Iblis to be a disbeliever, and He informed that he had fixed his heart upon it at the time of refusal.
